topics.title: Bohr's model: postulates, radius and energy

learn.hook: In 1913 Niels Bohr took Rutherford's collapsing atom and added one bold rule: electrons may only live in certain orbits. The atom stopped collapsing, and hydrogen's spectrum made sense.
points: Postulates: (1) the electron moves round the nucleus in circular orbits of fixed radius and energy (stationary states or energy levels), numbered n = 1, 2, 3, ...; (2) energy does not change while the electron stays in an orbit; (3) energy is absorbed or emitted only when the electron jumps between orbits, with ν = ΔE/h (Bohr frequency rule); (4) angular momentum is quantised: mₑvr = nh/2π.
Radius of the nth orbit of hydrogen: rₙ = 52.9 n² pm (n = 1 gives the Bohr radius a₀ = 52.9 pm). For hydrogen-like ions: rₙ = 52.9 (n²/Z) pm.
Energy of the nth level: Eₙ = −R_H (1/n²) with R_H = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. For hydrogen-like ions (He⁺, Li²⁺, Be³⁺): Eₙ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ (Z²/n²) J.

Negative energy means the electron is bound: a free electron at rest, infinitely far from the nucleus (n = ∞), has zero energy. As n decreases the energy becomes more negative and the electron is more strongly bound; n = 1 is the most stable (ground) state.
Higher Z pulls electrons closer (smaller r) and binds them more tightly (more negative E).

learn.reallife: Bohr's model is how neon signs on Mumbai's Marine Drive are explained in class: electrons jump up when current passes, then fall back and emit light of specific colours.

topics.title: Bohr's explanation of the hydrogen spectrum and its limits

learn.hook: Bohr's formula predicted hydrogen's lines to several decimal places, a stunning success. Yet put a second electron in the atom and the model falls apart.
points: Energy gap between levels: ΔE = Ef − Ei = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ (1/nᵢ² − 1/nf²) J. ΔE is negative for emission (nf < nᵢ) and positive for absorption (nf > nᵢ).
Frequency of the line: ν = |ΔE|/h = 3.29 × 10¹⁵ (1/nf² − 1/nᵢ²) Hz for emission; wavelength λ = c/ν; wavenumber ν̄ = 1.09677 × 10⁷ (1/nf² − 1/nᵢ²) m⁻¹.
Ionisation energy of hydrogen from the ground state = energy to move the electron from n = 1 to n = ∞ = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J per atom (about 1312 kJ mol⁻¹).

Limitations: Bohr's model cannot explain the fine structure (doublets) of hydrogen lines, the spectra of multi-electron atoms such as helium, the splitting of lines in a magnetic field (Zeeman effect) or in an electric field (Stark effect), or why atoms form molecules with definite shapes.
Its deeper flaw, shown later by de Broglie and Heisenberg, is that an electron cannot have a precisely defined orbit.

example.q: Calculate the energy released when an electron in hydrogen falls from n = 5 to n = 2.
steps: = −4.578 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (negative: energy is emitted)
ν = 4.578 × 10⁻¹⁹/6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ = 6.91 × 10¹⁴ Hz; λ = c/ν ≈ 434 nm (violet Balmer line)

learn.reallife: Sodium-vapour street lamps on Indian highways glow yellow-orange because of a doublet of very close lines near 589 nm. That pair of lines is exactly the kind of fine structure Bohr's model could not explain.

topics.title: Dual nature of matter and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle

learn.hook: If light can behave like particles, can particles behave like waves? A young Louis de Broglie said yes in 1924, and electron microscopes now image viruses because he was right.
points: de Broglie (1924): every moving particle has a wavelength λ = h/mv = h/p, where p = mv is momentum. Heavier or faster particles have shorter wavelengths.
Evidence: a beam of electrons undergoes diffraction just like X-rays, a wave property. The electron microscope uses the wave nature of electrons and magnifies about 15 million times.
For everyday objects λ is far too small to detect: a 0.1 kg cricket ball at 10 m s⁻¹ has λ = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ m. Wave effects matter only for tiny masses like electrons.
Heisenberg's uncertainty principle (1927): it is impossible to know exactly and simultaneously both the position and the momentum (or velocity) of an electron. Δx × Δp ≥ h/4π, or Δx × Δv ≥ h/4πm.
The more precisely we fix position (small Δx), the larger the uncertainty in momentum (large Δp), and vice versa.

example.q: Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) moving at 1.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).
steps: λ = h/mv
example.answer: About 0.73 nm, comparable to X-ray wavelengths

learn.reallife: IISc Bengaluru and AIIMS run cryo-electron microscopes that use electron waves to reveal the 3-D shapes of proteins and viruses, something no light microscope could resolve.

topics.title: Uncertainty in action and the Schrödinger equation

learn.hook: Heisenberg's principle quietly destroyed Bohr's neat circular orbits. In their place Schrödinger wrote one equation that still underlies every chemistry simulation run on India's PARAM supercomputers.
points: Significance: an exact orbit means knowing an electron's position and velocity together, which the uncertainty principle forbids. So we can only speak of the probability of finding an electron at a point. For large objects the uncertainty is negligible.

Calculation: Δv ≥ h/(4π m Δx). For an electron located within 0.1 Å (10⁻¹¹ m), Δv ≈ 5.79 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, huge compared with its speed. For a 40 g golf ball the uncertainty in position is about 10⁻³³ m, utterly negligible.
Bohr's model fails because it ignores the dual (wave) nature of the electron and contradicts the uncertainty principle by assuming fixed orbits.

Quantum mechanics (Heisenberg and Schrödinger, 1926) treats the electron as a wave. Schrödinger's equation is Ĥψ = Eψ, where Ĥ is the Hamiltonian operator, ψ the wave function and E the total energy. Solving it gives the allowed energy levels and the corresponding wave functions.
For the hydrogen atom the equation gives energy levels and wave functions labelled by quantum numbers. An atomic orbital is the wave function ψ of one electron in an atom.

example.q: An electron is located within Δx = 0.1 Å = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Estimate the minimum uncertainty in its velocity (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, π = 3.1416).
steps: Δv = h/(4π m Δx)
example.answer: About 5.79 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, so the electron's path cannot be pinned down

learn.reallife: Drug-design start-ups in Bengaluru solve approximate Schrödinger equations on computers to predict how a molecule will bind to a protein before anyone synthesises it.

topics.title: Orbitals and the four quantum numbers

learn.hook: Every seat in a stadium has a stand, row, seat number and direction it faces. Every electron in an atom has a similar four-part address: its quantum numbers.
points: Features of the quantum mechanical model: electron energy is quantised; exact position and momentum cannot be known together; ψ itself has no physical meaning, but ψ² (|ψ|²) gives the probability density of finding the electron at a point.

Principal quantum number n = 1, 2, 3, ... gives the shell (K, L, M, N), size and, for hydrogen, the energy. Azimuthal quantum number l = 0 to n − 1 gives the subshell and shape: l = 0, 1, 2, 3 are s, p, d, f.
Magnetic quantum number mₗ = −l, ..., 0, ..., +l gives the orientation; a subshell has (2l + 1) orbitals and a shell has n² orbitals.
Spin quantum number mₛ = +½ or −½ (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1925): the electron spins clockwise or anticlockwise. An orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin, so a shell holds at most 2n².

Orbit versus orbital: an orbit is Bohr's definite circular path (planar, can hold up to 2n² electrons, contradicts the uncertainty principle); an orbital is a 3-D region of high probability described by ψ (holds at most 2 electrons, consistent with quantum mechanics).

example.q: List all subshells and the number of orbitals and electrons possible for n = 3.
steps: Orbitals: 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 = n²
Electrons: 2 × 9 = 18 = 2n²

learn.reallife: MRI scanners at AIIMS work by flipping the spins of hydrogen nuclei in a magnetic field, the same kind of 'up or down' spin idea that the spin quantum number gives electrons.

topics.title: Valid quantum numbers, orbital shapes and nodes

learn.hook: A p orbital looks like a dumbbell, but the electron is never found exactly at the nucleus between the lobes. Places with zero probability are called nodes, and you can count them with simple formulas.
points: Checking a set (n, l, mₗ, mₛ): l must be 0 to n − 1, mₗ must be between −l and +l, mₛ must be +½ or −½. (3, 2, −2, +½) is valid; (2, 2, 0, +½) is not (l cannot equal n); (3, 1, −2, −½) is not (|mₗ| > l).
Orbital shapes are shown by probability density plots or by boundary surface diagrams, which enclose a region where the probability of finding the electron is high (about 90%).

s orbitals are spherical, and their size grows with n (1s < 2s < 3s). p orbitals (from n = 2) are dumbbell-shaped with two lobes; the three p orbitals px, py, pz point along the x, y and z axes and are equal in energy and shape.

d orbitals (from n = 3) are five in number: dxy, dyz, dxz (lobes between the axes), dx²−y² (lobes along the x and y axes) and dz² (two lobes along z with a doughnut-shaped ring around the middle). In an isolated atom all five have equal energy.
Nodes: radial nodes = n − l − 1; angular nodes (nodal planes) = l; total nodes = n − 1. Example: 3p has 1 radial node and 1 angular node.

example.q: Find radial, angular and total nodes for 4d.
steps: Radial = n − l − 1 = 4 − 2 − 1 = 1
Angular = l = 2
Total = n − 1 = 3 (check: 1 + 2 = 3)

learn.reallife: The colour of a ruby or of Rajasthan's blue pottery glaze comes from electrons jumping between d orbitals of chromium or cobalt ions, which only makes sense once you know how d orbitals are shaped and oriented.

games.title: Valid or invalid set (n, l, mₗ, mₛ)?

quiz.q: Which set of quantum numbers (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) is NOT possible?
quiz.explain: For n = 2, l can only be 0 or 1, so l = 2 is impossible.
steps: Rule: l ≤ n − 1
Check (2, 2, 1, +½): n = 2, l = 2 → l must be 0 or 1, so impossible
The other sets obey all the rules
Answer: (2, 2, 1, +½)
quiz.mistake: Forgets that l must be less than n

quiz.q: Which set of quantum numbers could describe an electron in a 4f orbital?
quiz.explain: 4f means n = 4 and l = 3; mₗ = −2 lies within −3 to +3.
steps: 4f means n = 4 and l = 3
mₗ must be between −3 and +3; −2 is allowed
"n = 4, l = 4, mₗ = 1, mₛ = +½" has l = 4 (> n − 1); n = 3 with l = 3 is impossible too
Answer: n = 4, l = 3, mₗ = −2, mₛ = +½
quiz.mistake: Uses l = 2 for f, or lets l equal n

quiz.q: How many radial nodes does a 3p orbital have?
quiz.explain: Radial nodes = n − l − 1 = 3 − 1 − 1 = 1.
steps: Answer: 1
quiz.mistake: Uses n − 1, which gives total nodes

quiz.q: How many angular nodes (nodal planes) does a d orbital have?
quiz.explain: Angular nodes = l, and l = 2 for d orbitals.
steps: Rule: angular nodes = l
For d orbitals, l = 2
So 2 angular nodes
Answer: 2
quiz.mistake: Confuses angular nodes with radial nodes

quiz.q: Which d orbital has its lobes lying along the x and y axes?
quiz.explain: dx²−y² points along the axes; dxy, dyz and dxz have lobes between the axes.
steps: dx²−y² has lobes along the x and y axes
dxy, dyz and dxz have lobes between the axes
Answer: dx²−y²
quiz.mistake: Assumes dxy lies along x and y because of its label

quiz.q: What is the shape of an s orbital?
quiz.explain: s orbitals are spherically symmetric; the probability depends only on distance from the nucleus.
steps: An s orbital's probability depends only on distance from the nucleus
So it is spherically symmetric
Dumbbell shape is p
Answer: Spherical
quiz.mistake: Confuses s with p orbitals

quiz.q: What does a boundary surface diagram of an orbital represent?
options: A region where the electron is never found
A surface enclosing a region where the probability of finding the electron is high, about 90%
The exact path of the electron
quiz.explain: It encloses most of the electron density; it is a picture of where the electron is likely to be, not a path.
steps: A boundary surface encloses the region where the electron is likely to be
It holds about 90% of the probability
It is not a path
Answer: A surface enclosing a region where the probability of finding the electron is high, about 90%
quiz.mistake: Treats the boundary surface as an orbit

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A 2s orbital has one radial node. Reason (R): Radial nodes = n − l − 1.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: For 2s, n − l − 1 = 2 − 0 − 1 = 1, so there is one spherical node.
steps: Radial nodes = n − l − 1
So one radial node: A and R true, R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks s orbitals never have nodes

teach.ask: Gappu found the set (2, 2, 0, +½) in a book. 'Is it allowed? And how do I count nodes in 3p?'
teach.praise: Perfect! l must be less than n, so that set is impossible, and 3p has n − l − 1 = 1 radial and l = 1 angular node. Gappu is now a node detective!
teach.nudge: Good! What is the maximum value of l for n = 2, and what formulas give radial and angular nodes?

revise.summary: A set of quantum numbers is valid only if l < n, |mₗ| ≤ l and mₛ = ±½. s orbitals are spherical, p are dumbbells, d come in five shapes, and nodes follow simple formulas.
focus: Check whether a quantum number set is valid
Shapes and orientations of s, p and d orbitals
Count radial, angular and total nodes
remember: Radial nodes = n − l − 1; angular nodes = l; total = n − 1
dx²−y² lobes lie along x and y axes; dxy, dyz, dxz lie between axes
Boundary surface encloses about 90% probability
traps: Don't use n − 1 for radial nodes; that is total nodes
Don't assume dxy lies along the x and y axes
Don't treat a boundary surface as an orbit

topics.title: Orbital energies, the (n + l) rule, Aufbau and Pauli

learn.hook: Why does potassium put its 19th electron in 4s instead of 3d? The answer is a tug-of-war between nuclear attraction and shielding by inner electrons.
points: In hydrogen, orbital energy depends only on n: 1s < 2s = 2p < 3s = 3p = 3d < 4s = 4p = 4d = 4f. Orbitals of equal energy are called degenerate.

In multi-electron atoms, inner electrons shield (screen) outer ones, so an outer electron feels an effective nuclear charge Z_eff less than Z. Orbitals that penetrate closer to the nucleus feel more Z_eff; penetration order s > p > d > f, so energy now depends on both n and l: 2s < 2p, 3s < 3p < 3d.

(n + l) rule: the lower the value of (n + l), the lower the energy. If two orbitals have the same (n + l), the one with lower n has lower energy. Order: 1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d < 4p < 5s < 4d < 5p < 6s < 4f < 5d < 6p < 7s.
Aufbau principle: in the ground state, orbitals are filled in order of increasing energy.
Pauli exclusion principle (1926): no two electrons in an atom can have all four quantum numbers the same. So an orbital holds at most 2 electrons, with opposite spins, and a shell holds at most 2n².

example.q: Use the (n + l) rule to decide which fills first: 4p or 5s; 4f or 5d.
steps: 4p: 4 + 1 = 5; 5s: 5 + 0 = 5. Equal, so lower n (4p) fills first.
4f: 4 + 3 = 7; 5d: 5 + 2 = 7. Equal, so lower n (4f) fills first.

learn.reallife: Seating at a crowded Mumbai local works like Aufbau: people fill the most convenient seats first and, like Pauli's rule, only two can squeeze onto a single seat facing opposite ways.

quiz.q: Which orbital is filled first according to the (n + l) rule?
quiz.explain: 4s has n + l = 4, lower than 3d (5), 4p (5) and 4d (6).
steps: Lowest (n + l) fills first → 4s
Answer: 4s
quiz.mistake: Assumes lower n always fills first

quiz.q: Between 3d and 4p (both n + l = 5), which has lower energy and why?
options: 3d, because it has the lower n
4p, because it has the lower l
quiz.explain: When n + l is equal, the orbital with lower n has lower energy.
steps: Rule: if (n + l) is equal, the lower n has lower energy
So 3d is lower
Answer: 3d, because it has the lower n
quiz.mistake: Uses l instead of n to break the tie

quiz.q: In a hydrogen atom, how do the energies of 3s, 3p and 3d compare?
quiz.explain: With only one electron there is no shielding, so energy depends only on n; all n = 3 orbitals are degenerate.
steps: Hydrogen has only one electron, so no shielding
Energy then depends only on n
So 3s = 3p = 3d
Answer: All equal
quiz.mistake: Applies multi-electron ordering to hydrogen

quiz.q: Why is 2s lower in energy than 2p in a lithium atom?
options: 2s penetrates closer to the nucleus, so it feels a larger effective nuclear charge
quiz.explain: s electrons penetrate the inner shielding more than p electrons, so they are held more tightly and are lower in energy.
steps: In Li, 2s penetrates closer to the nucleus than 2p
It feels a larger effective nuclear charge
So 2s is lower in energy
Answer: 2s penetrates closer to the nucleus, so it feels a larger effective nuclear charge
quiz.mistake: Thinks orbitals with the same n must have the same energy in every atom

quiz.q: What is the maximum number of electrons with n = 3 and mₛ = +½ in an atom?
quiz.explain: n = 3 has n² = 9 orbitals; each orbital can hold one electron with mₛ = +½, so 9.
steps: Orbitals for n = 3: 3² = 9
One +½ electron per orbital → 9
Answer: 9
quiz.mistake: Gives 2n² = 18, counting both spins

quiz.q: Which statement is the Pauli exclusion principle?
options: Electrons pair up only after each degenerate orbital has one electron
Position and momentum cannot both be known exactly
Electrons fill orbitals of lowest energy first
No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers
quiz.explain: This limits each orbital to 2 electrons of opposite spin. The other options describe Aufbau, Hund's rule and Heisenberg.
steps: Pauli: no two electrons in an atom can have all four quantum numbers the same
"Electrons pair up only after each degenerate orbital has one electron" is Hund's rule; the others are Heisenberg's principle and the Aufbau rule
Answer: No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the three filling rules

quiz.q: What is the effective nuclear charge?
options: The net positive charge actually felt by an electron after shielding by other electrons
The total charge of the nucleus
The charge of all electrons together
quiz.explain: Inner electrons shield outer ones from the full nuclear charge, so Z_eff < Z for outer electrons.
steps: Inner electrons shield outer electrons from the full nuclear charge
The net charge actually felt is the effective nuclear charge, Z_eff < Z
Answer: The net positive charge actually felt by an electron after shielding by other electrons
quiz.mistake: Thinks every electron feels the full nuclear charge

quiz.q: Assertion (A): In potassium, the 19th electron enters 4s rather than 3d. Reason (R): The (n + l) value of 4s is lower than that of 3d.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: 4s has n + l = 4 and 3d has 5, so 4s is lower in energy and fills first: K is [Ar]4s¹.
steps: Lower (n + l) → 4s fills before 3d
So K = [Ar]4s¹: A and R true, R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Fills 3d first because 3 is less than 4

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'Why does 4s fill before 3d? And how many electrons can one orbital hold?'
teach.praise: Excellent! 4s has the lower n + l, Aufbau fills lowest energy first, and Pauli allows only two electrons of opposite spin per orbital. Gappu's orbitals are neatly filled!
teach.nudge: Nearly! Compare n + l for 4s and 3d, and tell Gappu what the Pauli principle limits each orbital to.

revise.summary: In hydrogen, orbital energy depends only on n, but in multi-electron atoms shielding makes it depend on n and l. Orbitals fill by the (n + l) rule and the Aufbau principle, and Pauli limits each orbital to two electrons.
focus: Apply the (n + l) rule and its tie-break
Explain shielding, penetration and effective nuclear charge
State Aufbau and Pauli principles
remember: Lower (n + l) fills first; if equal, lower n first
Order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p 6s 4f 5d 6p 7s
Pauli: no two electrons in an atom have all four quantum numbers the same
traps: Don't assume lower n always fills first (4s before 3d)
Don't apply multi-electron ordering to hydrogen; there 3s = 3p = 3d
Don't think every electron feels the full nuclear charge

topics.title: Hund's rule, electronic configurations and extra stability

learn.hook: Chromium 'should' be 3d⁴4s², yet it is 3d⁵4s¹. Electrons will happily break the expected pattern for the comfort of a half-filled set.
points: Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity: in degenerate orbitals (p, d, f), electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins before any pairing begins. Pairing in p starts with the 4th electron, in d with the 6th, in f with the 8th.
Electronic configuration is written in spdf notation (N: 1s² 2s² 2p³) or with orbital boxes. Noble gas core notation shortens it: Na = [Ne] 3s¹, Fe = [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s².
Core electrons fill the inner, completed shells; valence electrons in the outermost shell take part in bonding. For first-30 elements: K [Ar]4s¹, Ca [Ar]4s², Sc [Ar]3d¹4s², ... Zn [Ar]3d¹⁰4s².

Exceptions: Cr = [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. Half-filled and completely filled subshells are extra stable because of their symmetrical distribution of electrons and their larger exchange energy (more pairs of parallel-spin electrons can exchange positions).
For cations, remove electrons from the outermost shell first: Fe²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁶ (4s electrons leave first), Fe³⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁵. Count unpaired electrons using Hund's rule.

example.q: Write the configuration of Mn (Z = 25) and Mn²⁺ and count unpaired electrons in each.
steps: Mn: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s²; the five 3d electrons sit singly in five orbitals → 5 unpaired.
Mn²⁺: remove the two 4s electrons → [Ar] 3d⁵.
3d⁵ again has 5 unpaired electrons, all with parallel spins (a stable half-filled set).

learn.reallife: The blue of copper sulphate solution in a school lab and the green of nickel salts both come from partly filled d subshells: Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹ and Ni²⁺ is 3d⁸. Colourless zinc salts (Zn²⁺, 3d¹⁰) show what a completely filled d subshell does.

quiz.q: What is the electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24)?
quiz.explain: One 4s electron moves to 3d to give a half-filled 3d⁵ subshell, which is extra stable.
steps: Expected Cr (Z = 24): [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s²
One 4s electron moves to 3d → half-filled 3d⁵, extra stable
So [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹
Answer: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹
quiz.mistake: Applies the Aufbau order blindly

quiz.q: How many unpaired electrons are in an Fe³⁺ ion (Z of Fe = 26)?
quiz.explain: Fe = [Ar]3d⁶4s². Fe³⁺ loses two 4s and one 3d electron: [Ar]3d⁵ with 5 unpaired electrons.
steps: Fe: [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²
Remove 4s² first, then one 3d
Fe³⁺: 3d⁵ → 5 unpaired
Answer: 5
quiz.mistake: Removes 3d electrons before 4s electrons

quiz.q: Which electronic configuration obeys Hund's rule for the 2p electrons of nitrogen?
options: One 2p orbital with two paired electrons and one with a single electron
All three electrons in one 2p orbital
Three 2p orbitals each with one electron, all spins parallel
Two electrons in 2s and none in 2p
quiz.explain: Hund's rule: electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing.
steps: N has 3 electrons in the three 2p orbitals
Hund's rule: fill degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing
So one electron in each 2p orbital, spins parallel
Answer: Three 2p orbitals each with one electron, all spins parallel
quiz.mistake: Pairs electrons too early

quiz.q: What is the configuration of Cu⁺ (Z of Cu = 29)?
quiz.explain: Cu = [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹; removing the single 4s electron leaves [Ar]3d¹⁰.
steps: Cu (Z = 29) = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹
Cu⁺ loses one electron, taken from 4s
Cu⁺ = [Ar] 3d¹⁰
Answer: [Ar] 3d¹⁰
quiz.mistake: Removes a 3d electron instead of the 4s electron

quiz.q: Why are half-filled and completely filled subshells extra stable?
options: Symmetrical electron distribution and larger exchange energy
They contain no electrons with parallel spins
quiz.explain: Symmetry lowers repulsion effects, and more parallel-spin electrons can exchange positions, giving more exchange energy and stability.
steps: Half-filled and filled subshells have a symmetrical electron distribution
More parallel-spin electrons can exchange places, giving larger exchange energy
Answer: Symmetrical electron distribution and larger exchange energy
quiz.mistake: Thinks extra stability comes from the nucleus

quiz.q: How many electrons are in the valence shell of sulphur (Z = 16)?
quiz.explain: S = [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴; the valence shell (n = 3) holds 2 + 4 = 6 electrons.
steps: S: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴
Answer: 6
quiz.mistake: Counts all electrons or only the p electrons

quiz.q: How many electrons in a ground-state chlorine atom (Z = 17) have l = 1?
quiz.explain: l = 1 means p electrons: 2p⁶ + 3p⁵ = 11.
steps: Cl: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵
p electrons = 6 + 5 = 11
Answer: 11
quiz.mistake: Counts only the outer 3p electrons

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Copper has the configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. Reason (R): A completely filled d subshell is extra stable.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: One 4s electron shifts to 3d to complete it, gaining extra stability from symmetry and exchange energy.
steps: Expected Cu: [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s²
One 4s electron moves to complete 3d¹⁰, which is extra stable
So [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹: A and R true, R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Writes Cu as [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s² following plain Aufbau

teach.ask: Gappu writes Cr as [Ar]3d⁴4s². 'My teacher marked it wrong! Why? And what is Hund's rule?'
teach.praise: Superb! Cr is 3d⁵4s¹ for a stable half-filled set with high exchange energy, and Hund says fill singly with parallel spins first. Gappu gets full marks now!
teach.nudge: Close! What is special about 3d⁵, and how should electrons fill degenerate orbitals according to Hund?

revise.summary: Hund's rule fills degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing. Configurations are written in spdf or noble gas notation, with Cr and Cu as exceptions due to the extra stability of half-filled and filled subshells.
focus: Write configurations for the first 30 elements
Remember the Cr and Cu exceptions and why
Write configurations of cations
Count unpaired electrons
remember: Cr = [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹; Cu = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹
Extra stability: symmetrical distribution and larger exchange energy
Cations lose outermost (4s) electrons first: Fe²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁶
traps: Don't remove 3d electrons before 4s when forming cations
Don't pair electrons before each degenerate orbital has one
Don't write Cu as [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s²

chapters.title: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

topics.title: Why classify? Triads, octaves and early tables

learn.hook: By 1865 chemists knew 63 elements and had no map. Every attempt to organise them was like sorting a cricket team by jersey colour until someone found the real pattern.
points: Classification lets us study elements systematically: instead of memorising each one, we learn trends and families. Only 31 elements were known in 1800; 63 by 1865; 118 today.

Johann Döbereiner (1829) found triads: groups of three similar elements in which the middle element's atomic weight is about the mean of the other two. Li (7), Na (23), K (39): (7 + 39)/2 = 23. Others: Ca–Sr–Ba and Cl–Br–I. The idea worked only for a few elements.
A. E. B. de Chancourtois (1862), a French geologist, arranged elements by atomic weight on a cylinder (the telluric helix), showing periodic recurrence of properties. His work drew little attention.

John Newlands (1865) proposed the law of octaves: when elements are arranged by increasing atomic weight, every eighth element has properties like the first, like musical notes. It held only up to calcium. He was later awarded the Davy Medal (1887).
Lothar Meyer (1869) plotted physical properties such as atomic volume, melting point and boiling point against atomic weight and obtained a periodically repeating pattern.

example.q: Check whether Ca (40), Sr (88) and Ba (137) form a Döbereiner triad.
steps: Mean of the end elements = (40 + 137)/2 = 177/2 = 88.5
Atomic weight of Sr = 88
88.5 ≈ 88, so the rule holds approximately.

learn.reallife: Online grocery apps group products into categories so you can find anything quickly. Classification of elements does the same for 118 elements.

games.title: Who proposed what?
pairs: Atomic volume vs atomic weight curves
Periodic law based on atomic weight

items.q: Every ___th element is similar in Newlands' octaves

quiz.q: Li (7), Na (23) and K (39) form a Döbereiner triad. What is the mean of the atomic weights of Li and K?
quiz.explain: (7 + 39)/2 = 23, equal to the atomic weight of sodium.
steps: Answer: 23
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 2

quiz.q: Newlands' law of octaves worked well only up to which element?
quiz.explain: Beyond calcium the 'every eighth element' pattern broke down, so the law was not widely accepted.
steps: Newlands: every eighth element resembles the first (law of octaves)
The pattern held for lighter elements but broke down after calcium
Answer: Calcium
quiz.mistake: Thinks the law worked for all known elements

quiz.q: Which scientist plotted atomic volumes against atomic weights and found a periodic pattern?
quiz.explain: Lothar Meyer (1869) showed that physical properties such as atomic volume vary periodically with atomic weight.
steps: Lothar Meyer (1869) plotted atomic volume against atomic weight
The curve showed a periodic pattern of physical properties
Answer: Lothar Meyer
quiz.mistake: Confuses Lothar Meyer with Moseley, who worked with X-rays

quiz.q: What was the main limitation of Döbereiner's triads?
options: Only a few such triads could be found among known elements
They predicted too many new elements
quiz.explain: The triad rule fitted only a handful of element groups, so it could not organise all elements.
steps: Döbereiner: middle element's atomic weight ≈ mean of the other two
Only a few such triads could be found
So the rule could not organise all elements
Answer: Only a few such triads could be found among known elements
quiz.mistake: Thinks triads were based on atomic number

quiz.q: The telluric helix, which arranged elements by atomic weight on a cylinder, was proposed by:
quiz.explain: French geologist de Chancourtois proposed the cylindrical arrangement in 1862.
steps: The telluric helix arranged elements by atomic weight on a cylinder
It was proposed by the French geologist de Chancourtois in 1862
Answer: Chancourtois
quiz.mistake: Credits Newlands, whose idea was the law of octaves

quiz.q: Why did chemists in the 19th century need to classify elements?
options: The growing number of elements made it hard to study each one separately
To reduce the number of elements
To decide the price of elements
quiz.explain: A classification groups similar elements so that properties can be studied as trends and families.
steps: More and more elements were being discovered
Studying each separately became hard, so similar elements were grouped
Answer: The growing number of elements made it hard to study each one separately
quiz.mistake: Thinks classification changes elements themselves

quiz.q: Cl (35.5), Br (80) and I (127) form a triad. How close is Br's atomic weight to the mean of Cl and I?
quiz.explain: (35.5 + 127)/2 = 81.25, which is close to 80, so the triad roughly holds.
steps: Mean of Cl and I = (35.5 + 127) ÷ 2
Br = 80, which is close to 81.25
So the triad roughly holds
Answer: The mean is 81.25, close to 80
quiz.mistake: Adds without dividing, or claims an exact match

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Newlands compared his arrangement with musical notes. Reason (R): He found that every eighth element resembled the first, like the eighth note of an octave.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The repeat after seven steps reminded Newlands of a musical octave, which gave the law its name.
steps: Check A: Newlands compared his arrangement with musical notes: true
Check R: every eighth element resembled the first, like an octave: true
R explains A: the repeat after seven steps suggested the musical octave
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the octave refers to eight groups in the modern table

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What were Döbereiner's triads and Newlands' octaves, and why were they not enough?'
teach.praise: Great! Triads had a middle element at the average weight, octaves repeated every eighth element, but both failed beyond a few elements. Gappu sees why Mendeleev was needed!
teach.nudge: Nice! What pattern did each one find, and why could neither organise all the elements?

revise.summary: Chemists classified elements to study them systematically. Early attempts were Döbereiner's triads, Chancourtois's telluric helix, Newlands' law of octaves and Lothar Meyer's property plots.
focus: Match each early idea to its scientist and year
Check a triad by averaging the outer atomic weights
State the limitation of triads and of octaves
remember: Döbereiner (1829): triads, e.g. Li (7), Na (23), K (39)
Newlands (1865): law of octaves, held only up to calcium
Chancourtois (1862): telluric helix; Lothar Meyer (1869): atomic volume vs atomic weight
traps: Don't forget to divide by 2 when finding the triad mean
Don't credit Newlands with the telluric helix; it was Chancourtois
Don't think the law of octaves worked for all elements

topics.title: Mendeleev's periodic law and his bold predictions

learn.hook: Mendeleev described elements nobody had seen, giving their densities and formulas of their oxides. Years later gallium and germanium turned up almost exactly as he predicted.
points: Mendeleev's periodic law (1869): the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic weights.

He arranged elements in horizontal rows and vertical columns in order of increasing atomic weight so that elements with similar properties fell in the same column, and he gave more weight to similarity of properties (such as formulas of oxides and hydrides) than to strict order of weight.

Boldness: he left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties. Eka-aluminium became gallium (predicted atomic weight 68, density 5.9 g cm⁻³, oxide E₂O₃; actual Ga: 70, 5.94 g cm⁻³, Ga₂O₃). Eka-silicon became germanium (predicted 72, oxide EO₂, chloride ECl₄; actual Ge: 72.6, GeO₂, GeCl₄).
He also corrected some atomic weights that did not fit, trusting the periodic pattern over doubtful measurements.

Anomalies: some elements had to be placed out of atomic-weight order (iodine, 127, after tellurium, 128, so that iodine sat with the halogens); isotopes, having different atomic weights, should have needed different places; and hydrogen had no fixed position.

example.q: Why did Mendeleev place iodine (127) after tellurium (128), breaking his own atomic-weight order?
steps: Iodine's properties resemble chlorine and bromine (halogens).
Tellurium's properties resemble sulphur and selenium.
Keeping similar elements in the same group mattered more to him than strict weight order.
example.answer: To keep iodine in the halogen group and tellurium with sulphur and selenium

learn.reallife: A good IPL scout leaves a slot open for a player type the team lacks and describes exactly what kind of player should fill it. Mendeleev did that for gallium and germanium.

games.title: Mendeleev's table: true or false?
items: Mendeleev arranged elements in order of increasing atomic number
He used atomic weight; atomic number was not known in 1869.
He left gaps for elements still to be discovered
Iodine was placed after tellurium even though its atomic weight is smaller
Similarity of properties was given priority.
Mendeleev's table had a definite place for isotopes of an element
Isotopes differ in atomic weight, which his system could not accommodate.
Gallium's measured density was very close to Mendeleev's prediction for eka-aluminium
Predicted 5.9 g cm⁻³; found 5.94 g cm⁻³.

quiz.q: Mendeleev's periodic law states that properties of elements are a periodic function of their:
quiz.explain: In 1869 Mendeleev based his law on atomic weights; atomic numbers came with Moseley in 1913.
steps: Mendeleev's law (1869) was based on atomic weights
Atomic numbers came later with Moseley (1913)
"Atomic numbers" is the modern periodic law, not Mendeleev's

topics.title: Moseley, the modern periodic law and the long form table

learn.hook: A 26-year-old Henry Moseley fired electrons at metals and measured the X-rays. One straight-line graph fixed the inverted pairs that had bothered Mendeleev for 40 years.
points: Moseley (1913) found that the square root of the frequency of X-rays emitted by an element (√ν) gives a straight line when plotted against atomic number Z, but not against atomic mass. So atomic number is the more fundamental property.
Modern periodic law: the physical and chemical properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
Arranged by atomic number, the inverted pairs (Te 52 before I 53; Ar 18 before K 19; Co 27 before Ni 28) fall in the correct order naturally.

The long form of the periodic table has 7 horizontal periods and 18 vertical groups, numbered 1 to 18 as recommended by IUPAC. Period numbers equal the highest principal quantum number of the elements.
The 14 lanthanoids (Ce to Lu, Z = 58–71) and 14 actinoids (Th to Lr, Z = 90–103) are placed in separate rows at the bottom to keep the table compact.

example.q: Explain how the modern periodic law resolves the position of argon (Ar, 39.9) before potassium (K, 39.1).
steps: By atomic weight, K (39.1) should come before Ar (39.9).
By atomic number, Ar has Z = 18 and K has Z = 19.
Ordering by Z places Ar with the noble gases and K with the alkali metals, matching their properties.

learn.reallife: Just as Aadhaar replaced name-based records with a unique number for every person, the atomic number became each element's unique ID, ending confusion caused by atomic weights.

topics.title: IUPAC names for elements with Z above 100

learn.hook: When element 118 was first made, nobody could agree on who discovered it, so it needed a neutral placeholder name. IUPAC's answer: 'ununoctium', built from numbers alone.
points: For newly made elements with Z > 100, IUPAC gives a temporary systematic name built from numerical roots of the digits of Z, followed by the ending -ium.
Roots: 0 = nil (n), 1 = un (u), 2 = bi (b), 3 = tri (t), 4 = quad (q), 5 = pent (p), 6 = hex (h), 7 = sept (s), 8 = oct (o), 9 = enn (e).
The symbol is made from the first letters of the roots (three letters). Examples: 101 unnilunium (Unu), 104 unnilquadium (Unq), 118 ununoctium (Uuo), 120 unbinilium (Ubn).
Spelling tweaks: the final 'i' of bi and tri is dropped before -ium (bium, trium); the final 'n' of enn is dropped before nil (ennil).
After discovery is confirmed, IUPAC approves an official name and symbol: 101 is mendelevium (Md), 104 rutherfordium (Rf), 118 oganesson (Og).

example.q: Write the IUPAC temporary name and symbol for Z = 113.
steps: Digits: 1, 1, 3 → un + un + tri
Add -ium; 'tri' loses its 'i': un + un + trium
Name: ununtrium; symbol from first letters: U, u, t

learn.reallife: Element 113, nihonium, honours Japan, where it was made. New superheavy elements are created only in large accelerators, a field Indian scientists contribute to through international collaborations.

topics.title: Electronic configuration, periods and groups

learn.hook: Give any element's atomic number and you can find its exact seat in the periodic table, the way an IRCTC PNR leads you to coach and berth.
points: The period number equals the principal quantum number (n) of the outermost (valence) shell. Each new period begins a new shell: period 1 fills 1s, period 2 fills 2s and 2p, and so on.

Number of elements in each period = number of electrons that can be placed in the orbitals being filled: 2 (1s), 8 (2s, 2p), 8 (3s, 3p), 18 (4s, 3d, 4p), 18 (5s, 4d, 5p), 32 (6s, 4f, 5d, 6p) and 32 in period 7 (7s, 5f, 6d, 7p).
Elements in a group have the same valence-shell configuration, which is why they show similar chemistry: all group 1 elements end in ns¹, all halogens in ns² np⁵.

Finding the position: block = last subshell to receive an electron; period = highest n; group = number of ns electrons (s-block), number of (n−1)d + ns electrons (d-block), or 10 + number of ns + np electrons (p-block).
Example rules at work: Z = 17 is [Ne] 3s² 3p⁵ → p-block, period 3, group 10 + 7 = 17 (chlorine).

example.q: Locate the element with Z = 26 in the periodic table.
steps: Configuration: [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²
Last electron enters 3d → d-block
Highest n = 4 → period 4
Group = 6 (3d) + 2 (4s) = 8 → group 8 (iron)

learn.reallife: In the electronics industry around Noida, engineers dope silicon (group 14) with phosphorus (group 15) or boron (group 13). Knowing group numbers tells them instantly which adds extra electrons and which creates holes.

p-block group = 10 + 6 = 16

topics.title: s, p, d and f blocks; metals, non-metals and metalloids

learn.hook: Sodium in your salt, chlorine in tap water disinfection, iron in the Delhi Metro tracks and neodymium in phone speakers: four blocks of the periodic table in one day.
points: s-block (groups 1 and 2): ns¹ (alkali metals) and ns² (alkaline earth metals). Reactive metals with low ionisation enthalpies; they lose electrons readily to form 1+ and 2+ ions. Their compounds are mostly ionic, except those of lithium and beryllium. Metallic character and reactivity increase down the group.

p-block (groups 13–18): ns² np¹ to ns² np⁶. Together, s- and p-block elements are the representative or main group elements. Group 18 (noble gases, ns² np⁶; He 1s²) have closed shells and very low reactivity. Group 16 elements are the chalcogens and group 17 the halogens; non-metallic character increases across a period and decreases down a group.

d-block (groups 3–12): (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns⁰⁻² (e.g. Pd is 4d¹⁰ 5s⁰). Transition elements: all metals, mostly form coloured ions, show variable valence (oxidation states), paramagnetism and catalytic activity. Zn, Cd and Hg ((n−1)d¹⁰ ns²) lack most transition properties.

f-block (inner transition elements): lanthanoids (Ce, Z = 58 to Lu, Z = 71) and actinoids (Th, Z = 90 to Lr, Z = 103), filling (n−2)f orbitals. Actinoids are radioactive; elements after uranium (Z = 92) are transuranium elements, mostly made artificially in tiny amounts.
Metals (more than 78% of known elements) lie on the left; non-metals at the top right. Metalloids such as Si, Ge, As, Sb and Te lie along the zig-zag border and show properties of both.

Si ([Ne]3s²3p²): p-block metalloid

Answer: Elements with atomic number greater than 92
quiz.mistake: Includes uranium itself or the lanthanoids

quiz.q: Why do s-block elements rarely occur free in nature?
options: They are highly reactive and readily lose their valence electrons
quiz.explain: Low ionisation enthalpies make alkali and alkaline earth metals very reactive, so they occur as compounds.
steps: s-block metals have low ionisation enthalpies
They lose valence electrons easily, so they are very reactive
So they occur as compounds, not free
Answer: They are highly reactive and readily lose their valence electrons
quiz.mistake: Thinks they are unreactive

quiz.q: Which element is a d-block element but does NOT show typical transition-metal properties?
quiz.explain: Zn has a completely filled 3d¹⁰ subshell in its atom and its common ion, so it lacks colour and variable valence.
steps: Zn has a completely filled 3d¹⁰ in its atom and in Zn²⁺
With no partly filled d orbitals it shows no colour or variable valence
Answer: Zinc
quiz.mistake: Assumes every d-block element behaves like a typical transition metal

quiz.q: The elements from Z = 90 to Z = 103 are known as:
quiz.explain: Thorium (90) to lawrencium (103) are the actinoids, filling 5f orbitals.
steps: Thorium (90) to lawrencium (103) fill 5f orbitals
These are the actinoids
Answer: Actinoids
quiz.mistake: Confuses actinoids (5f) with lanthanoids (4f)

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Noble gases are chemically very unreactive. Reason (R): Their valence shells are completely filled (ns² np⁶; He 1s²).
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Closed shells give very high ionisation enthalpies and little tendency to gain electrons, so reactivity is very low.
steps: Check A: noble gases are very unreactive: true
Check R: their valence shells are full (ns² np⁶; He 1s²): true
R explains A: closed shells give high ionisation enthalpy and little electron gain
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks noble gases are unreactive because they are gases

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What makes s, p, d and f blocks different, and where do metals and non-metals sit?'
teach.praise: Superb! Blocks are named by the subshell receiving the last electron, d-block metals show colour and variable valence, metals sit left and non-metals right. Gappu can now read the table's neighbourhoods!
teach.nudge: Nice! How is a block decided, what is special about d-block elements, and where are the metals and non-metals?

revise.summary: The table is divided into s, p, d and f blocks by the last subshell filled, each with typical properties. Metals lie on the left, non-metals top right, and metalloids along the zig-zag border.
focus: Configurations and properties of each block
Typical transition metal properties and the Zn, Cd, Hg exception
Name group families: chalcogens (16), halogens (17), noble gases (18)
Identify metalloids
remember: d-block: coloured ions, variable oxidation states, paramagnetism, catalytic activity
Transuranium: Z greater than 92
Metalloids: Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te

Don't assume every d-block element is a typical transition metal; zinc is not

topics.title: Atomic and ionic radii, and isoelectronic species

learn.hook: Lose an electron and you shrink a lot: a sodium atom has a radius of 186 pm, but Na⁺ has only 95 pm. Size explains half of the periodic table's behaviour.
points: Properties vary periodically because valence-shell configurations repeat at regular intervals of atomic number.

Atomic radius is measured as covalent radius (half the distance between two bonded atoms in a molecule: Cl₂ bond 198 pm → r(Cl) = 99 pm) or metallic radius (half the distance between neighbouring nuclei in a metal crystal: Cu–Cu 256 pm → 128 pm).

Across a period atomic radius decreases: electrons enter the same shell while nuclear charge increases, pulling them closer. Down a group it increases: a new shell is added each time and inner electrons shield the outer ones.

A cation is smaller than its atom (fewer electrons, same nuclear charge, often a lost shell): Na 186 pm, Na⁺ 95 pm. An anion is larger than its atom (extra electrons repel and Z_eff per electron falls): F 64 pm, F⁻ 136 pm.
Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons. Among them, the higher the nuclear charge, the smaller the radius: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺ (all 10 electrons).

example.q: Arrange in decreasing radius: Mg²⁺, O²⁻, Na⁺, F⁻, N³⁻.
steps: All have 10 electrons (isoelectronic).
Nuclear charges: N 7, O 8, F 9, Na 11, Mg 12.
Smaller Z means weaker pull on the same 10 electrons, so a larger ion.

learn.reallife: Water filters that soften hard water in Indian homes swap Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ for Na⁺ on ion-exchange resins; the size and charge of these ions decide how strongly the resin holds them.

games.title: Size trends: true or false?
items: Atomic radius generally decreases from left to right across a period
Nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell.
A cation is larger than its parent atom
Losing electrons makes it smaller; Na⁺ (95 pm) is much smaller than Na (186 pm).
Atomic radius increases down a group
A new shell is added for each period.
Among isoelectronic species, the one with the highest nuclear charge is the largest
Higher nuclear charge pulls the same electrons closer, making it the smallest.
The covalent radius of chlorine is half the Cl–Cl bond length

quiz.q: The Cl–Cl bond length in Cl₂ is 198 pm. What is the covalent radius of chlorine in pm?
quiz.explain: Covalent radius = half the internuclear distance = 198/2 = 99 pm.
steps: r = d/2
Answer: 99
quiz.mistake: Takes the whole bond length as the radius

quiz.q: The distance between neighbouring copper nuclei in copper metal is 256 pm. What is the metallic radius of copper in pm?
quiz.explain: Metallic radius = 256/2 = 128 pm.
steps: Answer: 128
quiz.mistake: Doubles the distance instead of halving it

quiz.q: Which has the largest radius?
quiz.explain: Radius increases down a group (K below Na below Li) and decreases across a period (Mg smaller than Na).
steps: Rule: radius increases down a group, decreases across a period
Li < Na < K down group 1
Mg is smaller than Na (same period, further right)
So K is largest
Answer: K
quiz.mistake: Ignores the effect of extra shells

quiz.q: Which correctly orders the radii of the isoelectronic ions?
quiz.explain: Same 10 electrons; nuclear charge rises O (8) < F (9) < Na (11) < Mg (12), so size falls in that order.
steps: O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺ each have 10 electrons
Nuclear charge: 8 < 9 < 11 < 12
More protons pull the same electrons closer, so size falls: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺
Answer: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺
quiz.mistake: Thinks positive ions are larger because they 'have more protons'

quiz.q: Why is the F⁻ ion (136 pm) much larger than the F atom (64 pm)?
options: The added electron increases repulsion and lowers the effective nuclear charge per electron
F⁻ has an extra shell of protons
Fluorine atoms are always measured incorrectly
quiz.explain: Ten electrons are held by the same nine protons, so the electron cloud expands.
steps: F has 9 electrons; F⁻ has 10 with the same 9 protons
The extra electron adds repulsion and lowers Z_eff per electron
So the electron cloud expands
Answer: The added electron increases repulsion and lowers the effective nuclear charge per electron
quiz.mistake: Thinks gaining an electron makes a species smaller

quiz.q: Why does atomic radius decrease from Na to Cl across period 3?
options: Electrons are removed across the period
Nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell
A new shell is added for each element
quiz.explain: Effective nuclear charge rises and shielding by electrons in the same shell is poor, so the electron cloud is pulled inwards.
steps: Across period 3, each element adds a proton and an electron to the same shell
Electrons in the same shell shield poorly, so Z_eff rises
The cloud is pulled inwards, radius falls
Answer: Nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell
quiz.mistake: Thinks shells are added across a period

quiz.q: Which pair consists of isoelectronic species?
quiz.explain: Na⁺ has 11 − 1 = 10 electrons, the same as Ne.
steps: Isoelectronic = same number of electrons
Na⁺: 11 − 1 = 10 electrons; Ne: 10 electrons
So Na⁺ and Ne
K⁺ has 18 and Cl⁻ has 18, F⁻ has 10
Answer: Na⁺ and Ne
quiz.mistake: Compares species with different electron counts

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Mg²⁺ is smaller than Na⁺. Reason (R): Mg²⁺ has a higher nuclear charge acting on the same number of electrons.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both have 10 electrons; 12 protons in Mg²⁺ pull them closer than 11 protons in Na⁺.
steps: Mg²⁺: 12 protons, 10 electrons; Na⁺: 11 protons, 10 electrons
More protons pull the same electrons closer
So Mg²⁺ is smaller: A and R true, R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the larger charge on Mg²⁺ makes it larger

quiz.q: Why do properties such as atomic radius and ionisation enthalpy repeat at regular intervals of atomic number?
options: Atomic mass increases by a fixed amount each time
Valence-shell electronic configurations repeat at regular intervals
Every element has the same number of shells
quiz.explain: Elements with the same valence-shell configuration (such as ns¹ or ns² np⁵) recur after 2, 8, 8, 18, 18 and 32 elements, so their properties recur too.
steps: Properties depend on valence-shell configuration
Configurations like ns¹ or ns² np⁵ recur after 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 elements
So properties recur too
Answer: Valence-shell electronic configurations repeat at regular intervals
quiz.mistake: Links periodicity to atomic mass or neutrons instead of electronic configuration

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why is Na⁺ so much smaller than Na, why is F⁻ bigger than F, and how do I compare ions like O²⁻ and Mg²⁺?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! Cations shrink and anions swell, and for isoelectronic ions the higher nuclear charge wins with the smallest size. Gappu now sizes up ions like a pro!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens to size when electrons are lost or gained, and what decides size among ions with the same number of electrons?

revise.summary: Atomic radius decreases across a period and increases down a group. Cations are smaller and anions larger than their atoms, and among isoelectronic species higher nuclear charge means smaller size.
focus: Find covalent and metallic radius as half the distance
Explain radius trends across and down
Compare atom and ion sizes
Order isoelectronic species by size
remember: Covalent radius = half the bond length (Cl₂ 198 pm → 99 pm)
Isoelectronic: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺
Cation smaller than atom; anion larger than atom
traps: Don't take the whole bond length as the radius
Don't think shells are added across a period
Don't think a higher positive charge makes an ion larger

topics.title: Ionisation enthalpy: trends and anomalies

learn.hook: It takes 2372 kJ to pull one electron off each atom in a mole of helium, but only 376 kJ for caesium. That six-fold gap explains why caesium explodes in water and helium does nothing at all.
points: Ionisation enthalpy (ΔᵢH) is the energy needed to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻. Unit: kJ mol⁻¹. It is always positive (energy is absorbed).

Successive ionisation enthalpies always increase (ΔᵢH₂ > ΔᵢH₁), because removing an electron from a positive ion is harder. A very large jump appears when an electron is removed from a noble-gas core.
Trend across a period: generally increases (higher effective nuclear charge, smaller size). Noble gases have the highest values in each period and alkali metals the lowest.
Trend down a group: decreases, because atomic size increases and inner electrons shield the outer electron from the nucleus.

Anomalies: Be (899) > B (801) because B's 2p electron is less penetrating and better shielded than Be's 2s electron; N (1402) > O (1314) because N has a stable half-filled 2p³, while in O one 2p orbital holds a pair whose mutual repulsion makes one electron easier to remove.

example.q: Explain why the first ionisation enthalpy of Mg (738 kJ mol⁻¹) is higher than that of Al (577 kJ mol⁻¹).
steps: Mg: [Ne] 3s². The electron removed is a 3s electron.
Al: [Ne] 3s² 3p¹. The electron removed is a 3p electron.
A 3p electron penetrates less and is shielded by the 3s electrons, so it is held less tightly and is easier to remove.
example.answer: Al loses a less penetrating, better shielded 3p electron, so its ΔᵢH₁ is lower

learn.reallife: Caesium's very low ionisation enthalpy is why it is used in photoelectric cells: even visible light carries enough energy to knock out its loosely held outer electron.

games.title: Element and first ionisation enthalpy (kJ mol⁻¹)

quiz.q: Which equation represents the first ionisation enthalpy of sodium?
quiz.explain: Ionisation enthalpy is defined for an isolated gaseous atom losing one electron.
steps: Definition: energy to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom
For sodium: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻
"Na(g) + e⁻ → Na⁻(g)" is electron gain; Na(s) → Na(g) is sublimation
Answer: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻
quiz.mistake: Uses solid or aqueous states, or confuses it with electron gain

quiz.q: Why is the first ionisation enthalpy of nitrogen higher than that of oxygen?
options: O has a smaller nuclear charge
O has a completely filled 2p subshell
N has a stable half-filled 2p³ configuration; O's paired 2p electrons repel each other
quiz.explain: Removing an electron from O relieves pairing repulsion and leaves a half-filled 2p³; N's half-filled set is extra stable.
steps: N: 2p³, half-filled and extra stable
O: 2p⁴, one pair of electrons repel each other
Removing one from O is easier, so N has higher ΔᵢH₁
Answer: N has a stable half-filled 2p³ configuration; O's paired 2p electrons repel each other
quiz.mistake: Expects a smooth increase across the period with no exceptions

quiz.q: Why is ΔᵢH₁ of boron lower than that of beryllium?
options: B has fewer protons than Be
The 2p electron of B is less penetrating and more shielded than the 2s electron of Be
quiz.explain: B loses a 2p electron, which is shielded by the 2s electrons; Be loses a 2s electron that penetrates closer to the nucleus.
steps: Be loses a 2s electron, which penetrates close to the nucleus
B loses a 2p electron, shielded by the 2s electrons
So boron's ΔᵢH₁ is lower
Answer: The 2p electron of B is less penetrating and more shielded than the 2s electron of Be
quiz.mistake: Thinks Be has fewer protons, or calls 2s² half-filled

quiz.q: An element has ΔᵢH₁ = 520, ΔᵢH₂ = 7297 and ΔᵢH₃ = 11 810 kJ mol⁻¹. In which group is it most likely?
quiz.explain: The huge jump after the first electron shows that only one electron lies outside a noble-gas core: an alkali metal (this is lithium).
steps: Jump: ΔᵢH₂ / ΔᵢH₁ = 7297 / 520 ≈ 14, a huge jump
So only one electron lies outside a noble-gas core
One valence electron → group 1
Answer: Group 1
quiz.mistake: Counts the number of values given instead of locating the big jump

quiz.q: Which element has the lowest first ionisation enthalpy?
quiz.explain: Ionisation enthalpy decreases down group 1; Cs is the largest atom with the most shielding.
steps: Rule: ionisation enthalpy decreases down group 1
Order: Li > Na > K > Cs
Cs is largest with most shielding, so lowest
Answer: Cs
quiz.mistake: Forgets the down-group trend

quiz.q: Why is ΔᵢH₂ of sodium much larger than its ΔᵢH₁?
options: The second electron is in a 4s orbital
The second electron must come from the stable noble-gas core of Na⁺ ([Ne])
quiz.explain: After losing 3s¹, Na⁺ has the neon configuration; removing an electron from the closed 2p⁶ shell needs far more energy.
steps: Na → Na⁺ leaves [Ne], a closed noble-gas core
The second electron must come from the stable 2p⁶ shell
So ΔᵢH₂ is far larger
Answer: The second electron must come from the stable noble-gas core of Na⁺ ([Ne])
quiz.mistake: Thinks successive ionisation enthalpies increase only slightly

quiz.q: Which period 2 element has the highest first ionisation enthalpy?
quiz.explain: Noble gases have completely filled shells and the highest ionisation enthalpies in their periods.
steps: Noble gases have completely filled shells
They have the highest ionisation enthalpy in their period
In period 2 that is neon
Answer: Neon
quiz.mistake: Picks fluorine as the 'most non-metallic' element

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Ionisation enthalpy decreases down a group. Reason (R): Atomic size and shielding by inner electrons increase down a group.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The outer electron is farther from the nucleus and better shielded, so less energy is needed to remove it.
steps: Check A: ionisation enthalpy decreases down a group: true
Check R: size and shielding increase down a group: true
R explains A: the outer electron is farther and better shielded
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the increase in nuclear charge down a group dominates

teach.ask: Gappu sees that oxygen's ionisation enthalpy is less than nitrogen's. 'Isn't it supposed to increase across the period?'
teach.praise: Excellent! The general trend increases across a period, but N's half-filled 2p³ is extra stable while O's paired electron is easier to remove. Gappu loves an exception explained!
teach.nudge: Close! What is special about nitrogen's 2p configuration, and what happens to a paired electron in oxygen?

revise.summary: Ionisation enthalpy is the energy to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom; it generally increases across a period and decreases down a group. Be > B and N > O are key anomalies.
focus: Write the correct ionisation equation with gaseous states
Explain trends across and down
Explain the Be/B and N/O anomalies
Use a big jump in successive values to find the group
remember: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻; always positive
ΔᵢH₂ > ΔᵢH₁; huge jump on removing a noble-gas core electron
N > O: half-filled 2p³; Be > B: 2p less penetrating than 2s
traps: Don't expect a smooth increase across a period with no exceptions
Don't count values given to find the group; find the big jump
Don't pick fluorine as highest in period 2; neon is

topics.title: Electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity

learn.hook: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, yet chlorine, not fluorine, releases the most energy when it gains an electron. Small size has a hidden cost.
points: Electron gain enthalpy (Δ_egH) is the enthalpy change when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom: X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g). If energy is released, Δ_egH is negative (exothermic). Halogens have large negative values; noble gases have large positive values because the electron must enter a new, higher shell.
Trends: Δ_egH generally becomes more negative across a period (higher effective nuclear charge, smaller size) and less negative down a group (larger size).

Anomaly: O (−141) and F (−328) have less negative values than S (−200) and Cl (−349). In the small n = 2 shell, the incoming electron suffers strong repulsion from the electrons already there. So Cl has the most negative electron gain enthalpy of all elements.

Electronegativity is a qualitative measure of the ability of an atom in a chemical compound to attract shared electrons to itself. It is not directly measurable; Linus Pauling's scale gives fluorine the highest value, 4.0.
Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group. High electronegativity goes with non-metallic character; low electronegativity with metallic character.

example.q: Arrange F, Cl, Br, I in order of (a) electronegativity and (b) negative electron gain enthalpy.
steps: (a) Electronegativity falls smoothly down the group: F > Cl > Br > I.
(b) Δ_egH values: F −328, Cl −349, Br −325, I −295 kJ mol⁻¹.
Most negative first: Cl > F > Br > I (fluorine is pushed below chlorine by repulsion in its small 2p subshell).
example.answer: (a) F > Cl > Br > I; (b) Cl > F > Br > I

learn.reallife: Fluoride toothpastes and the Teflon on non-stick tawas both rely on fluorine's very high electronegativity, which makes the C–F bond one of the strongest and least reactive in chemistry.

games.title: Electron gain and electronegativity: true or false?

They have positive values; the added electron must go into a new shell.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element on the Pauling scale
Electronegativity can be measured directly like ionisation enthalpy
It is a relative, qualitative property derived from other data.
Larger atoms hold shared electrons less strongly.

O is −141 and S is −200 kJ mol⁻¹, because of repulsion in oxygen's compact 2p subshell.

quiz.explain: Cl (−349 kJ mol⁻¹) beats F (−328) because the extra electron in fluorine's small 2p subshell is strongly repelled.

F's small 2p subshell repels the incoming electron strongly
So chlorine is the most negative
Answer: Chlorine

quiz.q: Why do noble gases have positive electron gain enthalpies?
options: The added electron must enter the next, higher shell, which is unfavourable
quiz.explain: With ns² np⁶ complete, a new electron must go into the (n + 1)s orbital, far from the nucleus, so energy must be supplied.
steps: Noble gases have ns² np⁶ complete
An added electron must enter the next shell, far from the nucleus
Energy must be supplied, so ΔegH is positive

quiz.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale?
quiz.explain: Fluorine has the value 4.0; caesium is among the least electronegative.
steps: Pauling scale: fluorine = 4.0, the highest
Answer: Fluorine

quiz.q: Electronegativity refers to the ability of an atom to:
options: Release energy on gaining an electron in the gaseous state
Attract shared electrons towards itself in a compound
Lose electrons in the gaseous state

"Release energy on gaining an electron in the gaseous state" describes electron gain enthalpy (isolated gaseous atom)
Answer: Attract shared electrons towards itself in a compound
quiz.mistake: Mixes up electronegativity and electron gain enthalpy

quiz.q: Why is the electron gain enthalpy of oxygen less negative than that of sulphur?
options: Oxygen's small size causes strong repulsion between the incoming electron and existing 2p electrons
quiz.explain: In the compact n = 2 shell, electron–electron repulsion is large; in sulphur's bigger n = 3 shell, the added electron is accommodated more easily.
steps: Oxygen's n = 2 shell is compact, so electron–electron repulsion is large
Sulphur's bigger n = 3 shell holds the extra electron more easily
So O is less negative
Answer: Oxygen's small size causes strong repulsion between the incoming electron and existing 2p electrons
quiz.mistake: Expects electron gain enthalpy to become steadily less negative from O to S

quiz.q: How do electronegativity and metallic character relate across a period?
options: Electronegativity decreases and metallic character increases
Electronegativity increases and metallic character decreases
quiz.explain: Moving right, atoms attract electrons more strongly and become less metallic, more non-metallic.
steps: Across a period, atoms attract electrons more strongly
So electronegativity increases and metallic character decreases
Answer: Electronegativity increases and metallic character decreases
quiz.mistake: Thinks metallic character increases with electronegativity

quiz.q: Arrange in order of decreasing (most negative first) electron gain enthalpy: O, S, F, Cl.
quiz.explain: Values: Cl −349, F −328, S −200, O −141 kJ mol⁻¹.
steps: Values (kJ mol⁻¹): Cl −349, F −328, S −200, O −141
Most negative first: Cl > F > S > O
Answer: Cl > F > S > O
quiz.mistake: Follows electronegativity order instead of measured Δ_egH values

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Fluorine has a less negative electron gain enthalpy than chlorine. Reason (R): Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both statements are true, but the reason for A is the strong electron–electron repulsion in fluorine's small 2p subshell, not its electronegativity.
steps: Check A: F has less negative ΔegH than Cl: true
Check R: F is more electronegative than Cl: true
But A is due to repulsion in F's small 2p subshell, not electronegativity
So both true, R does not explain A
Answer: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Links two true facts as cause and effect

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so why does chlorine release more energy on gaining an electron?'
teach.praise: Superb! Fluorine's tiny 2p subshell causes repulsion so chlorine's Δ_egH is more negative, while electronegativity is about shared electrons in compounds. Gappu is no longer confused!
teach.nudge: Good! What problem does fluorine's small size cause for an incoming electron, and how is electronegativity different from electron gain enthalpy?

revise.summary: Electron gain enthalpy is the enthalpy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron; halogens have large negative values. Electronegativity is an atom's ability to attract shared electrons, highest for fluorine.
focus: Trends in electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity
Why O and F are less negative than S and Cl
Why noble gases have positive Δ_egH
Electronegativity versus electron gain enthalpy
remember: Most negative Δ_egH: chlorine; highest electronegativity: fluorine (4.0, Pauling)
Δ_egH order: Cl > F > Br > I

topics.title: Valence, anomalous second-period elements and nature of oxides

learn.hook: Lithium behaves more like magnesium than like sodium, and aluminium oxide can neutralise both acids and bases. The periodic table has diagonal shortcuts and double agents.
points: Valence (oxidation state) is periodic: for s- and p-block elements it equals the number of valence electrons or 8 minus that number. Group 1 shows +1, group 2 +2, group 13 +3; group 15 −3 in hydrides; group 17 −1. Oxygen shows −2 in Na₂O but +2 in OF₂, because F is more electronegative.

Second-period elements (Li to F) differ from the rest of their groups because of very small size, high charge/radius ratio, high electronegativity and absence of d orbitals. Their maximum covalency is 4 (B in [BF₄]⁻), while Al can reach 6 ([AlF₆]³⁻). They also form strong pπ–pπ multiple bonds (C=C, C≡C, N≡N, C=O).
Diagonal relationship: Li resembles Mg, Be resembles Al and B resembles Si, because size and charge effects balance along the diagonal.
Reactivity is highest at the two extremes of a period: alkali metals (lose electrons easily, strong reducing agents) and halogens (gain electrons readily, strong oxidising agents).
Oxides change from basic on the left to acidic on the right: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH (basic); Cl₂O₇ + H₂O → 2HClO₄ (acidic). Middle oxides are amphoteric (Al₂O₃, As₂O₃) or neutral (CO, NO, N₂O).

example.q: Classify the period 3 oxides Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃, Cl₂O₇.
steps: Metals on the left give basic oxides: Na₂O (strongly basic), MgO (basic).
Al₂O₃ reacts with both acids and bases: amphoteric.
Non-metals on the right give acidic oxides: SiO₂ (weakly acidic), P₄O₁₀, SO₃, Cl₂O₇ (strongly acidic).
example.answer: Basic → amphoteric → acidic across the period

learn.reallife: Farmers in Kerala add lime (CaO, a basic oxide) to acidic soils, while sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from factories (acidic oxides) cause acid rain that damages the marble of the Taj Mahal.

quiz.q: What is the oxidation state of oxygen in OF₂?
quiz.explain: Fluorine is more electronegative and is always −1, so 2(−1) + x = 0 gives x = +2 for oxygen.
steps: F = −1 each, total −2
Answer: +2
quiz.mistake: Assumes oxygen is always −2

quiz.q: Which oxide is amphoteric?
quiz.explain: Aluminium oxide reacts with acids (forming Al³⁺ salts) and with bases (forming aluminates).
steps: An amphoteric oxide reacts with both acids and bases
Al₂O₃ forms Al³⁺ salts with acids and aluminates with bases
SO₃ and Cl₂O₇ are acidic; Na₂O is basic
Answer: Al₂O₃
quiz.mistake: Thinks every metal oxide is basic

quiz.q: Why is the maximum covalency of boron 4 while that of aluminium can be 6?
options: Boron has no d orbitals in its valence shell; aluminium can use 3d orbitals
quiz.explain: Second-period elements have only 2s and 2p orbitals (four orbitals), limiting covalency to 4.
steps: Boron (period 2) has only 2s and 2p: four orbitals → covalency up to 4
Aluminium can also use 3d orbitals → covalency up to 6
Answer: Boron has no d orbitals in its valence shell; aluminium can use 3d orbitals
quiz.mistake: Attributes the difference to the number of valence electrons

quiz.q: Which pair shows a diagonal relationship?
quiz.explain: Be (group 2, period 2) and Al (group 13, period 3) lie diagonally and have similar properties.
steps: Diagonal relationship: period 2 element resembles the next group's period 3 element
Be (group 2, period 2) and Al (group 13, period 3)
Answer: Be and Al
quiz.mistake: Picks elements from the same group or period

quiz.q: Which element forms the most strongly basic oxide in period 3?
quiz.explain: Basic character of oxides decreases across the period; Na₂O is the most basic.
steps: Basic character of oxides decreases across a period
Na is first in period 3
So Na₂O is the most basic
Answer: Sodium
quiz.mistake: Reverses the trend in oxide character

quiz.q: Arrange in increasing first ionisation enthalpy: Na, Mg, Al, Si.
quiz.explain: Values (kJ mol⁻¹): Na 496, Al 577, Mg 738, Si 786. Al is lower than Mg because its 3p electron is easier to remove.
steps: Values (kJ mol⁻¹): Na 496, Al 577, Mg 738, Si 786
Increasing order: Na < Al < Mg < Si
Al < Mg because Al's 3p electron is easier to remove
Answer: Na < Al < Mg < Si
quiz.mistake: Assumes a perfectly smooth increase across the period

quiz.q: Arrange in decreasing atomic radius: N, P, O, F.
quiz.explain: P is in period 3 (larger); across period 2 radius falls N > O > F.
steps: P is in period 3, so it is the largest
Across period 2 radius falls: N > O > F
So P > N > O > F
Answer: P > N > O > F
quiz.mistake: Ignores the extra shell in P

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Second-period elements form strong multiple bonds such as N≡N and C=O. Reason (R): Their small size allows effective sideways (pπ–pπ) overlap of p orbitals.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Small atoms come close enough for their p orbitals to overlap sideways strongly, giving stable π bonds.
steps: Check A: period 2 elements form strong multiple bonds (N≡N, C=O): true
Check R: small size allows effective pπ–pπ overlap: true
R explains A: strong sideways overlap gives stable π bonds
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks multiple bonding requires d orbitals

teach.praise: Fantastic! Diagonal neighbours match in size and charge, and oxides go from basic on the left through amphoteric to acidic on the right. Gappu now reads the table diagonally too!
teach.nudge: Nice! What is the name for Li–Mg similarity, and how does the nature of oxides change across a period?

Anomalous behaviour of second-period elements
Diagonal relationships
Classify oxides as basic, amphoteric, acidic or neutral

Diagonal pairs: Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si
Amphoteric: Al₂O₃, As₂O₃; neutral: CO, NO, N₂O

Don't think every metal oxide is basic; Al₂O₃ is amphoteric
Don't think multiple bonding needs d orbitals

topics.title: Lewis symbols, the octet rule and covalent bonds

learn.hook: Noble gases sit alone like toppers who need no study group. Every other atom bonds to imitate their full outer shell.
points: Atoms combine to reach a more stable, lower-energy arrangement. Only valence (outer-shell) electrons take part. A Lewis symbol shows them as dots round the element symbol: Na•, •C• with four dots, :Cl• with seven. The number of dots usually gives the group valence, or 8 minus it.

Kössel: highly electropositive metals lose electrons and highly electronegative non-metals gain electrons, forming ions with noble-gas configurations (Na → Na⁺ + e⁻; Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻). The electrostatic attraction between ions is an electrovalent (ionic) bond; electrovalence = number of unit charges on the ion.
Octet rule (Kössel and Lewis, 1916): atoms combine by transferring or sharing valence electrons so that each attains eight electrons in its valence shell (two for H, a duplet).

Langmuir (1919) refined Lewis's ideas and coined 'covalent bond': a bond formed by mutual sharing of electron pairs. One shared pair = single bond (Cl–Cl), two pairs = double bond (O=C=O), three pairs = triple bond (N≡N, H–C≡C–H).

example.q: Show the formation of CO₂ using the octet rule.
steps: C has 4 valence electrons; each O has 6.
C shares two pairs with each O.
Each O now has 4 shared + 4 lone electrons = 8; C has 8 shared electrons.
Structure: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each oxygen.
example.answer: O=C=O, two double bonds, every atom with an octet

learn.reallife: LPG (propane and butane) burns in Indian kitchens because its C–H and C–C covalent bonds rearrange with O₂ into the stronger C=O and O–H bonds of CO₂ and water, releasing energy.

games.title: Molecule and bond type
