quiz.q: According to Kössel, a bond between sodium and chlorine forms by:
options: Transfer of an electron from Na to Cl, giving Na⁺ and Cl⁻
Transfer of an electron from Cl to Na
quiz.explain: Electropositive Na loses an electron to become Na⁺ ([Ne]); Cl gains it to become Cl⁻ ([Ar]). Their attraction is the ionic bond.
steps: Kössel: bonds form by transfer of electrons
Na (electropositive) loses one electron → Na⁺ ([Ne])
Cl gains it → Cl⁻ ([Ar]); the ions attract
Answer: Transfer of an electron from Na to Cl, giving Na⁺ and Cl⁻
quiz.mistake: Reverses the direction of electron transfer

quiz.q: How many electrons are shared between the two nitrogen atoms in N₂?
quiz.explain: N≡N is a triple bond: three shared pairs = 6 electrons.
steps: Triple bond = 3 pairs
3 × 2 = 6 electrons
Answer: 6
quiz.mistake: Counts bonds instead of electrons

quiz.q: What is the electrovalence of calcium in CaO?
quiz.explain: Ca loses two electrons to form Ca²⁺, so its electrovalence is 2.
steps: Ca: [Ar] 4s², loses two electrons → Ca²⁺
Electrovalence = number of electrons lost = 2
So 2
Answer: 2
quiz.mistake: Confuses electrovalence with the group number written as II

quiz.q: Who coined the term 'covalent bond'?
quiz.explain: Langmuir (1919) refined the Lewis model and introduced the term covalent bond.
steps: Langmuir (1919) refined the Lewis model
He introduced the term covalent bond
Answer: Langmuir
quiz.mistake: Credits Kössel, who worked on ionic bonding

quiz.q: In the Lewis representation of Cl₂, how many lone pairs does each chlorine atom carry?
quiz.explain: Each Cl has 7 valence electrons; one is used in the bond pair, leaving 6 electrons = 3 lone pairs.
steps: 7 valence electrons
1 in the shared pair
6 left → 3 lone pairs
Answer: 3
quiz.mistake: Counts the shared pair as a lone pair

quiz.q: Which statement about the octet rule is correct?
options: Hydrogen also needs eight valence electrons
It applies only to ionic compounds
Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to have eight electrons in their valence shell
All atoms must have exactly eight electrons in total
quiz.explain: The rule concerns the valence shell only; hydrogen aims for a duplet, and the rule covers both ionic and covalent bonding.
steps: Octet rule: atoms gain, lose or share electrons to get eight in the valence shell
It covers ionic and covalent bonds; hydrogen aims for a duplet
Answer: Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to have eight electrons in their valence shell
quiz.mistake: Applies the rule to total electrons or to hydrogen

quiz.q: Which molecule contains a double bond?
quiz.explain: Ethene, H₂C=CH₂, has a C=C double bond. Ethane has single bonds and ethyne a triple bond.
steps: C₂H₄ (ethene): H₂C=CH₂ has a C=C double bond
C₂H₆ and CH₄ have only single bonds; C₂H₂ has a triple bond
Answer: C₂H₄
quiz.mistake: Confuses ethene with ethyne

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Noble gases rarely form compounds. Reason (R): They already have a stable octet (duplet for He) in their valence shell.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The stability of a complete valence shell is the idea behind the octet rule, and it explains the low reactivity of noble gases.
steps: Check A: noble gases rarely form compounds: true
Check R: they already have a stable octet (He a duplet): true
R explains A: a complete valence shell has no need to react
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks noble gases never form any compound at all

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why do atoms bond at all, and how is sharing different from transferring electrons?'
teach.praise: Excellent! Atoms bond to complete an octet, either by transferring electrons (ionic) or sharing pairs (covalent). Gappu now feels like a noble gas!
teach.nudge: Good! What configuration are atoms aiming for, and what is the difference between ionic and covalent bonding?

revise.summary: Atoms bond using valence electrons to reach a stable noble-gas arrangement, either by transferring electrons (ionic bond) or sharing pairs (covalent bond). Lewis symbols show valence electrons as dots.
focus: Draw Lewis symbols and simple Lewis structures
Kössel's ionic bonding and electrovalence
State the octet rule
Single, double and triple bonds as shared pairs
remember: Octet rule (Kössel and Lewis, 1916): atoms transfer or share electrons to get eight valence electrons (two for H)
Covalent bond: mutual sharing of electron pairs (term by Langmuir, 1919)
Electrovalence = number of unit charges on the ion
traps: Don't reverse electron transfer: Na loses, Cl gains
Don't count bonds instead of electrons; N≡N shares 6 electrons
Don't credit Kössel with the term 'covalent bond'; it was Langmuir

topics.title: Drawing Lewis structures, formal charge and octet limits

learn.hook: Ozone protects us from UV rays, yet its Lewis structure seems to give one oxygen a positive charge. Formal charge is the bookkeeping that settles which structure is best.
points: Method: (1) add valence electrons of all atoms (add one per negative charge, subtract one per positive charge); (2) place the least electronegative atom in the centre (H and F are always terminal); (3) draw single bonds; (4) complete octets on outer atoms with lone pairs; (5) if the central atom lacks an octet, convert lone pairs into multiple bonds.

Formal charge (FC) of an atom = (valence electrons) − (non-bonding electrons) − ½(bonding electrons). The sum of formal charges equals the charge on the species. The best structure has the smallest formal charges, with negative charges on more electronegative atoms.
In O₃ (central O with one double and one single bond): central O = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1; doubly bonded O = 6 − 4 − 2 = 0; singly bonded O = 6 − 6 − 1 = −1.

Limitations of the octet rule: incomplete octet (BeH₂ and BeCl₂ have 4 electrons round Be; BCl₃ and AlCl₃ have 6); odd-electron molecules (NO, NO₂); expanded octet with d orbitals for period 3 and beyond (PF₅ has 10 electrons round P, SF₆ has 12, and S in H₂SO₄ has 12).
Other drawbacks: noble gases do form compounds (XeF₂, KrF₂, XeOF₂); the octet theory says nothing about shapes of molecules or the energy and relative stability of molecules.

example.q: Draw the Lewis structure of the nitrite ion, NO₂⁻, and find the formal charges.
steps: Valence electrons: 5 (N) + 2 × 6 (O) + 1 (charge) = 18.
N in centre, single bonds to both O (4 electrons used); complete O octets (12 more, 16 used); put the last 2 on N.
N has only 6, so make one N=O double bond: O=N–O⁻ with one lone pair on N.
example.answer: [O=N–O]⁻ with one lone pair on N, two on the double-bonded O, three on the single-bonded O (FC −1)

learn.reallife: Sulphuric acid, the most-produced chemical in India's fertiliser plants, has sulphur with 12 electrons around it, a classic case where the octet rule simply does not hold.

quiz.q: What is the formal charge on the central oxygen atom in O₃?
quiz.explain: Central O: 6 valence − 2 non-bonding − ½(6 bonding) = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1.
steps: L = 2 (one lone pair)
S = 6 (one double + one single bond)
Answer: +1
quiz.mistake: Counts only one of the two bonds on the central atom

quiz.q: How many valence electrons must be shown in the Lewis structure of the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻?
steps: Charge 2−: +2
Total = 24
Answer: 24
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add electrons for the negative charge

quiz.q: How many electrons surround the central atom in BCl₃?
quiz.explain: B forms three single bonds (3 pairs) and has no lone pair: 6 electrons, an incomplete octet.
steps: Boron has 3 valence electrons and forms 3 B–Cl single bonds
Electrons around B = 3 bond pairs × 2 = 6, no lone pair
So 6: an incomplete octet
Answer: 6
quiz.mistake: Assumes every central atom reaches an octet

quiz.q: Which molecule has an expanded octet around its central atom?
quiz.explain: S in SF₆ has six bond pairs = 12 electrons, possible because sulphur can use its 3d orbitals.
steps: Expanded octet = more than 8 electrons on the central atom
SF₆: 6 bond pairs × 2 = 12 electrons on S, using 3d orbitals
BeCl₂ has only 4; NO is odd-electron
Answer: SF₆
quiz.mistake: Confuses an incomplete octet with an expanded one

quiz.q: Which is an odd-electron molecule?
quiz.explain: NO₂ has 5 + 12 = 17 valence electrons; an odd total means one atom cannot have an octet.
steps: Total 17 (odd)
Answer: NO₂
quiz.mistake: Assumes every stable molecule has an even number of electrons

quiz.q: In the best Lewis structure of NH₄⁺, what is the formal charge on nitrogen?
quiz.explain: N: 5 − 0 lone pair electrons − ½(8) = 5 − 4 = +1. The four H atoms each have FC 0, so the total is +1.
steps: Answer: +1
quiz.mistake: Counts the four bonds as lone pairs

quiz.q: Which is NOT a drawback of the octet theory?
options: It cannot explain the shapes of molecules
It says nothing about the relative stability of molecules
It fails for compounds like XeF₂
It explains why atoms such as Na and Cl form ions
quiz.explain: Explaining ion formation is a success of the octet idea. The other three are genuine drawbacks.
steps: Octet theory's drawbacks: no shapes, no relative stability, fails for XeF₂
Explaining why Na and Cl form ions is a success, not a drawback
Answer: It explains why atoms such as Na and Cl form ions
quiz.mistake: Picks a success of the theory as a limitation

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Among possible Lewis structures, the one with the lowest formal charges is usually the most stable. Reason (R): The sum of formal charges in a neutral molecule must be zero.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both statements are true, but R is a bookkeeping rule. A is true because structures with less charge separation have lower energy, not because charges add to zero.
steps: Check A: the structure with lowest formal charges is usually most stable: true
Check R: formal charges in a neutral molecule add to zero: true
But R is only bookkeeping; A is due to less charge separation
So both true, R does not explain A
Answer: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Links two true facts as cause and effect

teach.ask: Gappu drew O₃ and got charges on two oxygens. 'Is that right? And do all molecules really follow the octet rule?'
teach.praise: Superb! Formal charge = V − L − ½S gives +1 and −1 in O₃, and the octet rule breaks for BCl₃, NO and SF₆. Gappu's Lewis structures now pass inspection!
teach.nudge: Close! How do you calculate formal charge, and can you name a molecule with an incomplete, odd or expanded octet?

revise.summary: Lewis structures are drawn by counting valence electrons, placing the least electronegative atom in the centre and completing octets. Formal charges pick the best structure, and some molecules break the octet rule.

Calculate formal charges

Drawbacks of the octet theory
remember: FC = valence electrons − non-bonding electrons − ½(bonding electrons)
Incomplete octet: BeCl₂, BCl₃, AlCl₃; odd-electron: NO, NO₂; expanded: PF₅, SF₆, H₂SO₄
Central O in O₃ has formal charge +1
traps: Don't forget to add electrons for a negative charge (CO₃²⁻ has 24)
Don't assume every central atom reaches an octet
Don't confuse an incomplete octet with an expanded one

topics.title: Ionic bonding, lattice enthalpy and Fajans' rules

learn.hook: Making Na⁺ and Cl⁻ from atoms actually costs energy. Salt exists only because the ions then crowd into a crystal and release a huge lattice enthalpy.
points: An ionic bond forms easily when: the metal has a low ionisation enthalpy (forms a cation easily), the non-metal has a high negative electron gain enthalpy (forms an anion easily), and the resulting crystal has a high lattice enthalpy.
Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻ needs 495.8 kJ mol⁻¹; Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g) releases only 348.7 kJ mol⁻¹. The sum is endothermic, so ion formation alone does not explain stability.

Lattice enthalpy: the energy required to completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into its gaseous ions. For NaCl it is 788 kJ mol⁻¹. This large energy released when the lattice forms is what stabilises ionic solids.

No bond is 100% ionic. Fajans' rules: covalent character of an ionic bond increases when the cation is small, the anion is large, and the charges are high, because a small, highly charged cation polarises (distorts) the electron cloud of the anion.

A cation with an (n−1)dⁿ ns⁰ configuration (typical of transition metals) is more polarising than one of the same size and charge with a noble-gas configuration (ns² np⁶), because d electrons shield the nucleus poorly.

example.q: Arrange LiCl, NaCl and KCl in order of increasing covalent character.
steps: Anion is the same (Cl⁻); compare cations: Li⁺ < Na⁺ < K⁺ in size.
A smaller cation is more polarising.
So covalent character: KCl < NaCl < LiCl.

learn.reallife: Rock salt mined at Mandi in Himachal and sea salt from Tuticorin are both NaCl lattices. Its high lattice enthalpy is why salt melts only at about 801 °C, far hotter than any kitchen.

games.title: Ionic bonds and Fajans' rules: true or false?
items: Lattice enthalpy is the energy needed to separate one mole of an ionic solid into gaseous ions
Formation of Na⁺(g) and Cl⁻(g) from gaseous atoms releases energy overall
495.8 kJ is needed but only 348.7 kJ is released, so it is endothermic.
A larger anion is more easily polarised
Its outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and more easily distorted.
Covalent character increases as cation size increases
Smaller cations are more polarising, so covalent character increases as cation size decreases.
A high lattice enthalpy favours formation of an ionic compound

quiz.q: Which factor favours the formation of an ionic bond?
options: Low ionisation enthalpy of the metal
Positive electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal
High ionisation enthalpy of the metal
quiz.explain: A metal that loses electrons easily (low ΔᵢH), a non-metal that gains them readily (negative Δ_egH) and a high lattice enthalpy all favour ionic bonding.
steps: Ionic bonding is favoured by easy electron loss by the metal
Low ionisation enthalpy of the metal does this
High ΔᵢH, positive Δ_egH or low lattice enthalpy all oppose it
Answer: Low ionisation enthalpy of the metal
quiz.mistake: Reverses the effect of ionisation enthalpy

quiz.q: For sodium, ΔᵢH = 495.8 kJ mol⁻¹, and for chlorine, Δ_egH = −348.7 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the net enthalpy change for Na(g) + Cl(g) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g), in kJ mol⁻¹?
quiz.explain: 495.8 + (−348.7) = +147.1 kJ mol⁻¹: energy must be supplied, so lattice enthalpy is needed to explain stability.
steps: Net ΔH = ΔᵢH(Na) + Δ_egH(Cl)
= +147.1 kJ mol⁻¹
Positive, so the lattice enthalpy must supply the stability
Answer: 147.1
quiz.mistake: Adds the magnitudes or gets the sign wrong

quiz.q: What is lattice enthalpy?
options: Energy released when an atom gains an electron
Energy needed to melt one mole of an ionic solid
Energy required to separate one mole of an ionic solid completely into gaseous ions
Energy needed to vaporise a metal
quiz.explain: It measures how strongly ions are held in the crystal; NaCl's value is 788 kJ mol⁻¹.
steps: Lattice enthalpy = energy to separate 1 mol of ionic solid into gaseous ions
e.g. NaCl: 788 kJ mol⁻¹
Answer: Energy required to separate one mole of an ionic solid completely into gaseous ions
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with enthalpy of fusion

quiz.q: Which compound shows the greatest covalent character?
quiz.explain: Li⁺ is the smallest cation and I⁻ the largest, most polarisable anion, so LiI is the most covalent.
steps: Fajans: small cation + large anion → most covalent character
Li⁺ is the smallest cation; I⁻ is the largest, most polarisable anion
So LiI
Answer: LiI
quiz.mistake: Thinks the most electronegative anion gives the most covalent bond

quiz.q: Why is AlCl₃ more covalent than NaCl?
options: AlCl₃ has a higher lattice enthalpy
Al³⁺ is smaller and more highly charged, so it polarises Cl⁻ more
Al has a lower ionisation enthalpy
quiz.explain: A small cation with high charge has high polarising power, distorting the anion's electron cloud and increasing covalent character.
steps: Al³⁺ is smaller and has a higher charge (3+) than Na⁺ (1+)
So it has higher polarising power and distorts Cl⁻ more
So AlCl₃ is more covalent
Answer: Al³⁺ is smaller and more highly charged, so it polarises Cl⁻ more
quiz.mistake: Ignores the effect of charge in Fajans' rules

quiz.q: Cu⁺ and Na⁺ have similar sizes and the same charge. Why is CuCl more covalent than NaCl?
options: Cu⁺ (3d¹⁰) has poorly shielding d electrons, making it more polarising than Na⁺ (2s² 2p⁶)
quiz.explain: d electrons shield the nuclear charge less effectively than s and p electrons, so Cu⁺ distorts the anion more.
steps: Cu⁺ is 3d¹⁰; Na⁺ is 2s² 2p⁶
d electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly
So Cu⁺ polarises Cl⁻ more, making CuCl more covalent
Answer: Cu⁺ (3d¹⁰) has poorly shielding d electrons, making it more polarising than Na⁺ (2s² 2p⁶)
quiz.mistake: Thinks cations of equal size and charge always polarise equally

quiz.q: The lattice enthalpy of NaCl is 788 kJ mol⁻¹. Which statement follows?
options: 788 kJ is released when NaCl dissolves
788 kJ is released when Na atoms form Na⁺
788 kJ is needed to melt one mole of NaCl
788 kJ is needed to break one mole of solid NaCl into Na⁺(g) and Cl⁻(g)
quiz.explain: Lattice enthalpy refers to separating the solid into gaseous ions, not to melting or dissolving.
steps: Lattice enthalpy refers to NaCl(s) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g)
So 788 kJ is needed to break 1 mol of solid NaCl into gaseous ions
It is not about melting or dissolving
Answer: 788 kJ is needed to break one mole of solid NaCl into Na⁺(g) and Cl⁻(g)
quiz.mistake: Confuses lattice enthalpy with melting or solution enthalpy

quiz.q: Assertion (A): LiCl is more soluble in organic solvents than NaCl. Reason (R): The small Li⁺ ion polarises Cl⁻ strongly, giving LiCl more covalent character.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: More covalent character makes LiCl behave more like a covalent compound, so it dissolves better in less polar solvents such as ethanol.
steps: Check A: LiCl dissolves better in organic solvents than NaCl: true
Check R: small Li⁺ polarises Cl⁻ strongly, giving covalent character: true
R explains A: more covalent compounds dissolve in less polar solvents
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Assumes all alkali metal chlorides are equally ionic

teach.ask: Gappu learned that forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ costs energy. 'Then why does salt exist at all? And is any bond fully ionic?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! The big lattice enthalpy pays for ion formation, and Fajans' rules show small cations polarising large anions to add covalent character. Gappu is impressed by salt!

revise.summary: Ionic bonds form easily with low ionisation enthalpy, large negative electron gain enthalpy and high lattice enthalpy; lattice enthalpy is what stabilises ionic solids. Fajans' rules tell when an ionic bond gains covalent character.

Define lattice enthalpy (NaCl 788 kJ mol⁻¹)
Apply Fajans' rules to compare covalent character
remember: Lattice enthalpy: energy to separate one mole of ionic solid completely into gaseous ions
Fajans: small cation, large anion, high charges → more covalent character
(n−1)dⁿ ns⁰ cations polarise more than noble-gas-configuration cations
traps: Don't confuse lattice enthalpy with enthalpy of fusion
Don't think the most electronegative anion gives the most covalent bond; large anions do (LiI)
Don't ignore charge: Al³⁺ makes AlCl₃ more covalent than NaCl

topics.title: Bond length, bond angle, bond enthalpy and bond order

learn.hook: The N≡N triple bond needs 946 kJ mol⁻¹ to break. That is why air is 78% nitrogen that plants cannot use directly and why fixing nitrogen into urea takes so much energy.
points: Bond length: the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms, measured by spectroscopy or X-ray diffraction. Covalent radius = half the distance between two identical bonded atoms; van der Waals radius = half the distance between two identical non-bonded atoms in neighbouring molecules (for Cl: 99 pm and 180 pm).
Bond angle: the angle between the orbitals holding bonding electron pairs around the central atom, measured by spectroscopy. H–O–H in water is 104.5°.
Bond enthalpy: energy needed to break one mole of bonds of a type in gaseous molecules into separated gaseous atoms. H–H = 435.8, O=O = 498, N≡N = 946.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
In polyatomic molecules successive bonds break with different energies (H₂O: 502 then 427 kJ mol⁻¹), so we use the average (mean) bond enthalpy: (502 + 427)/2 = 464.5 kJ mol⁻¹ for O–H.

Bond order (Lewis) = number of bonds between two atoms: H₂ 1, O₂ 2, N₂ 3. Isoelectronic species have the same bond order (N₂, CO, NO⁺ all 3). As bond order increases, bond enthalpy increases and bond length decreases.

example.q: Arrange the C–C bonds in ethane, ethene and ethyne by length and by enthalpy.
steps: Bond orders: C–C (1), C=C (2), C≡C (3).
Higher bond order pulls atoms closer: lengths about 154, 134 and 120 pm.
Higher bond order needs more energy to break.
example.answer: Length: ethane > ethene > ethyne; enthalpy: ethyne > ethene > ethane

learn.reallife: Gas welders in Indian workshops use oxy-acetylene torches. Burning ethyne releases a lot of energy partly because its weak π bonds are replaced by very strong C=O and O–H bonds.

quiz.q: In H₂O, the first O–H bond needs 502 kJ mol⁻¹ and the second 427 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the average O–H bond enthalpy in kJ mol⁻¹?
steps: Answer: 464.5
quiz.mistake: Takes the total or only the first value

quiz.q: How does bond length change as bond order increases between the same two atoms?
quiz.explain: More shared electron pairs pull the nuclei closer, so bond length falls.
steps: More shared electron pairs pull the two nuclei closer
So bond length decreases as bond order increases
Answer: It decreases
quiz.mistake: Thinks more bonds push atoms apart

quiz.q: Which species has the same bond order as N₂?
quiz.explain: CO is isoelectronic with N₂ (14 electrons) and also has bond order 3.
steps: N₂ has 14 electrons and bond order 3
CO also has 6 + 8 = 14 electrons (isoelectronic)
So CO has bond order 3
Answer: CO
quiz.mistake: Assumes neighbours in the periodic table must have equal bond orders

quiz.q: The van der Waals radius of chlorine (180 pm) is larger than its covalent radius (99 pm) because:
options: It measures half the distance between non-bonded atoms in neighbouring molecules
Chlorine atoms expand in the solid
Van der Waals forces are stronger than covalent bonds
quiz.explain: Non-bonded atoms cannot approach as closely as bonded atoms that share electrons.
steps: Covalent radius: half the distance between bonded atoms sharing electrons
Van der Waals radius: half the distance between non-bonded atoms of neighbouring molecules
Non-bonded atoms cannot come as close
Answer: It measures half the distance between non-bonded atoms in neighbouring molecules
quiz.mistake: Thinks the larger radius means a stronger force

quiz.q: What is the bond angle H–O–H in a water molecule?
quiz.explain: Two lone pairs on oxygen squeeze the bond pairs closer than the tetrahedral 109.5°, giving 104.5°.
steps: O in H₂O has 2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs (tetrahedral arrangement, 109.5°)
Lone pairs repel more and squeeze the H–O–H angle
Answer: 104.5°
quiz.mistake: Uses the ideal tetrahedral or the ammonia angle

quiz.q: Which bond has the highest bond enthalpy?
quiz.explain: The triple bond in N₂ (946 kJ mol⁻¹) is far stronger than O=O (498) or H–H (435.8).
steps: Bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹): N≡N 946, O=O 498, H–H 435.8
F–F is weak
So N≡N is highest
Answer: N≡N
quiz.mistake: Expects the lightest molecule to have the strongest bond

quiz.q: What is the bond order between carbon and oxygen in CO₂?
quiz.explain: O=C=O has two double bonds; each C–O link has bond order 2.
steps: Structure of CO₂: O=C=O
Each C–O link is a double bond
Bond order = 2
Answer: 2
quiz.mistake: Adds both bonds together to get 4

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Bond enthalpy of N₂ is greater than that of O₂. Reason (R): N₂ has a higher bond order than O₂.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Bond order 3 (N₂) versus 2 (O₂); higher bond order means a stronger bond.
steps: N₂ bond order = 3; O₂ bond order = 2
Higher bond order → stronger bond → higher bond enthalpy
A and R true, R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks molecular mass determines bond strength

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why is N≡N so hard to break and shorter than O=O? What is bond order?'
teach.praise: Perfect! Higher bond order means a shorter, stronger bond, so N≡N beats O=O. Gappu now respects nitrogen!
teach.nudge: Good! How do bond length and bond enthalpy change as bond order goes up?

revise.summary: Bonds are described by bond length, bond angle, bond enthalpy and bond order. Higher bond order means a stronger, shorter bond.
focus: Define bond length, covalent and van der Waals radius
Calculate average bond enthalpy
Find bond order and relate it to length and enthalpy
remember: H–O–H angle in water = 104.5°
Average O–H bond enthalpy = (502 + 427)/2 = 464.5 kJ mol⁻¹
Bond order: H₂ 1, O₂ 2, N₂ 3; N₂, CO, NO⁺ all 3
traps: Don't think more bonds push atoms apart; bond length decreases
Don't add both bonds in CO₂; each C–O bond order is 2
Don't take only the first bond enthalpy as the average

topics.title: Resonance: canonical forms and the hybrid

learn.hook: A rhinoceros is not half dragon and half unicorn switching back and forth; it is one real animal that no single imaginary picture describes. Resonance hybrids work the same way.
points: When a single Lewis structure cannot explain a molecule's properties, it is represented by two or more structures called canonical (resonance) structures; the real molecule is the resonance hybrid, shown with ↔ between the forms.
Ozone: two canonical forms (O=O–O and O–O=O). Both O–O bonds in O₃ are actually equal, 128 pm, between a single O–O (148 pm) and a double O=O (121 pm).

Carbonate ion CO₃²⁻: three equivalent canonical forms; all three C–O bonds are identical. CO₂ is a hybrid of O=C=O, ⁻O–C≡O⁺ and ⁺O≡C–O⁻; its C–O length (115 pm) lies between C=O (121 pm) and C≡O (110 pm).
Resonance stabilises a molecule: the hybrid has lower energy than any single canonical form. The difference is the resonance energy.
Canonical forms have no real existence; the molecule does not flip between them, and there is no equilibrium among them. Only electron positions differ between canonical forms; atoms stay in place.

example.q: Why are all three C–O bonds in CO₃²⁻ the same length?
steps: Draw three canonical forms, each with one C=O and two C–O⁻ bonds, the double bond in a different position each time.
The real ion is a hybrid of all three.
Each C–O bond has partial double-bond character (bond order 1⅓), so all are identical.
example.answer: The double bond is delocalised over all three C–O bonds

learn.reallife: Limestone and marble (CaCO₃), used from the Taj Mahal to Rajasthan's Makrana quarries, owe the symmetry of their carbonate ions to resonance.

games.title: Resonance: true or false?
items: A molecule rapidly flips between its canonical forms
The molecule exists only as the hybrid; canonical forms are imaginary.
Both O–O bonds in ozone have the same length
Each is 128 pm, between single and double bond lengths.
The resonance hybrid has higher energy than any single canonical structure
The hybrid is more stable (lower energy); the difference is resonance energy.
Canonical structures differ only in the arrangement of electrons, not atoms
Moving atoms would give a different compound (an isomer).
CO₃²⁻ has three equivalent canonical forms
The double bond can be drawn to any one of three oxygens.

quiz.q: What is the bond order of each C–O bond in the carbonate ion?
quiz.explain: Four bonds (one double + two single) spread over three C–O links: 4/3 ≈ 1.33.
steps: Total bonds C to O = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4
Divided over 3 links = 4/3
Answer: 4/3
quiz.mistake: Uses ozone's value of 3/2

quiz.q: What is the bond order of each O–O bond in ozone?
quiz.explain: One double and one single bond shared over two O–O links: 3/2 = 1.5.
steps: Total bonds = 2 + 1 = 3
Answer: 1.5
quiz.mistake: Uses the carbonate value of 4/3

quiz.q: What is resonance energy?
options: The energy needed to break all bonds
The difference in energy between the most stable canonical form and the actual resonance hybrid
The energy of the highest canonical form
The energy released when canonical forms interconvert
quiz.explain: The real hybrid is lower in energy than even the most stable canonical form; the difference measures the extra stability.
steps: The real resonance hybrid is lower in energy than any canonical form
Resonance energy = energy of most stable canonical form − energy of the hybrid
Answer: The difference in energy between the most stable canonical form and the actual resonance hybrid
quiz.mistake: Thinks resonance means interconversion between real structures

quiz.q: Which statement about canonical structures is correct?
options: They have no real existence; the molecule is the hybrid
Each exists for a short time
They differ in the positions of atoms
quiz.explain: Canonical forms are only a way of describing delocalised electrons; atoms do not move between them.
steps: Canonical forms only describe delocalised electrons on paper
The molecule exists only as the hybrid; atoms do not move between forms
Answer: They have no real existence; the molecule is the hybrid
quiz.mistake: Treats canonical structures like tautomers in equilibrium

quiz.q: The C–O bond length in CO₂ (115 pm) lies between the C=O (121 pm) and C≡O (110 pm) lengths. This is explained by:
options: The presence of lone pairs on carbon
quiz.explain: Contributions from triple-bonded forms shorten the bond below a pure double bond.
steps: CO₂ C–O = 115 pm, between C=O (121 pm) and C≡O (110 pm)
Resonance forms with triple bonds (⁻O–C≡O⁺, ⁺O≡C–O⁻) contribute
So the bond is shorter than a pure double bond
Answer: Resonance among O=C=O, ⁻O–C≡O⁺ and ⁺O≡C–O⁻
quiz.mistake: Assumes the bonds in CO₂ are simple double bonds

quiz.q: In ozone, the single O–O bond length is 148 pm and the double O=O is 121 pm. The actual O–O bond length (128 pm) is:
options: Between the two, showing partial double-bond character
quiz.explain: The hybrid has bonds intermediate between single and double, confirming resonance.
steps: Ozone O–O = 128 pm
So it lies between: partial double-bond character
Answer: Between the two, showing partial double-bond character
quiz.mistake: Expects one long and one short bond

quiz.q: How many canonical structures are usually drawn for the carbonate ion?
quiz.explain: The C=O double bond can be placed on any of the three oxygen atoms.
steps: In CO₃²⁻ the C=O double bond can sit on any one of the 3 oxygens
So 3 canonical structures
Answer: 3
quiz.mistake: Draws only two forms as for ozone

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Benzene's six C–C bonds are all of equal length. Reason (R): Benzene is a resonance hybrid of two Kekulé structures.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Delocalisation makes every C–C bond intermediate (139 pm) between C–C and C=C.
steps: Check A: all six C–C bonds in benzene are equal (139 pm): true
Check R: benzene is a hybrid of two Kekulé structures: true
R explains A: delocalisation makes every bond intermediate
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks benzene has alternating single and double bonds

teach.ask: Gappu drew two structures for O₃ and asks: 'Does ozone keep switching between them?'
teach.praise: Superb! Ozone is one resonance hybrid, the canonical forms are imaginary, and both bonds are equal and intermediate. Gappu stops flipping!
teach.nudge: Close! Does the molecule really switch? What does the real molecule look like, and what do the bond lengths show?

revise.summary: When one Lewis structure is not enough, a molecule is shown as a resonance hybrid of canonical forms. The hybrid is more stable than any single form, and its bonds are of equal, in-between length.
focus: Draw canonical forms of O₃, CO₃²⁻ and CO₂
Explain equal bond lengths in O₃ and CO₃²⁻
Define resonance energy
Know that canonical forms are not real
remember: Bond order: O–O in O₃ = 1.5; C–O in CO₃²⁻ = 4/3
O–O in O₃ is 128 pm, between 148 pm (single) and 121 pm (double)
Resonance energy: energy difference between the most stable canonical form and the hybrid
traps: Don't think the molecule flips between canonical forms; they have no real existence
Don't mix up ozone's bond order (1.5) with carbonate's (4/3)
Don't move atoms between canonical forms; only electrons differ

topics.title: Polar bonds, dipole moment and molecular shape

learn.hook: Rub a comb on dry hair and bring it near a thin stream of tap water: the stream bends. Water molecules are tiny dipoles, and their shape is the reason.
points: Between identical atoms (H₂, Cl₂) the shared pair is equally shared: a non-polar covalent bond. Between atoms of different electronegativity, the pair shifts towards the more electronegative atom, creating partial charges δ⁺ and δ⁻: a polar covalent bond (H^δ⁺–F^δ⁻).

Dipole moment μ = charge (Q) × distance of separation (r). Unit: debye (D); 1 D = 3.33564 × 10⁻³⁰ C m. It is a vector, drawn as a crossed arrow (⟼) with the cross at the positive end, pointing towards the negative end.

In polyatomic molecules the net dipole moment is the vector sum of bond dipoles (and lone-pair contributions). Symmetrical shapes cancel bond dipoles: BeF₂ and CO₂ (linear), BF₃ (trigonal planar), CH₄ and CCl₄ (tetrahedral) all have μ = 0.
Bent H₂O (μ = 1.85 D) and pyramidal NH₃ have non-zero dipole moments, so a measured μ ≠ 0 rules out a linear or planar symmetrical shape.
NH₃ (1.47 D) has a larger μ than NF₃ (0.23 D): in NH₃ the lone-pair moment points the same way as the resultant N–H bond moments, but in NF₃ it opposes the N–F bond moments.

example.q: CO₂ and H₂O are both triatomic and both contain polar bonds. Why is μ(CO₂) = 0 but μ(H₂O) = 1.85 D?
steps: CO₂ is linear: the two C=O bond dipoles are equal and point in opposite directions, so they cancel.
H₂O is bent (104.5°): the two O–H bond dipoles add to give a resultant along the angle bisector.
Shape, not just bond polarity, decides the net dipole moment.
example.answer: Linear CO₂ cancels its bond dipoles; bent H₂O does not

learn.reallife: Microwave ovens heat food because polar water molecules keep rotating to follow the oscillating electric field; non-polar oils on their own warm far more slowly.

items.text: Dipole moment = charge × ___ of separation.
The unit of dipole moment is the ___.
In HF, the partial negative charge is on ___.
NH₃ has a ___ dipole moment than NF₃.

quiz.q: Which molecule has zero dipole moment?
quiz.explain: BF₃ is trigonal planar; three equal B–F bond dipoles at 120° cancel.
steps: BF₃ is trigonal planar
Three equal B–F bond dipoles at 120° add to zero
So μ = 0
H₂O and NH₃ are bent or pyramidal; HCl is polar
Answer: BF₃
quiz.mistake: Assumes any molecule with polar bonds must be polar

quiz.q: Why does NH₃ have a larger dipole moment than NF₃?
options: In NH₃ the lone pair moment adds to the bond moments; in NF₃ it opposes them
quiz.explain: In NH₃ the N–H bond dipoles point towards N, the same direction as the lone pair. In NF₃ the N–F dipoles point away from N, opposing the lone pair.
steps: NH₃: N–H dipoles point towards N, the same way as the lone pair → moments add
NF₃: N–F dipoles point towards F, opposing the lone pair → moments partly cancel
So NH₃ has the larger μ
Answer: In NH₃ the lone pair moment adds to the bond moments; in NF₃ it opposes them
quiz.mistake: Expects the more electronegative F to give the bigger dipole

quiz.q: A molecule AB₂ has a dipole moment of 1.85 D. What can you conclude about its shape?
quiz.explain: A linear AB₂ would cancel its bond dipoles; a non-zero μ shows the molecule is bent (as in H₂O).
steps: A linear AB₂ (B–A–B at 180°) would cancel its two bond dipoles → μ = 0
μ = 1.85 D ≠ 0, so the dipoles do not cancel
So the molecule is bent
Answer: It is bent, not linear
quiz.mistake: Thinks dipole moment gives no information about shape

quiz.q: Two charges of magnitude 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C are separated by 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. What is the dipole moment in units of 10⁻²⁹ C m?
steps: μ = Q × r
Answer: 1.6
quiz.mistake: Adds exponents wrongly

quiz.q: Which bond is the most polar?
quiz.explain: The electronegativity difference between H and F is the largest, so the bond is most polar.
steps: Bond polarity depends on electronegativity difference
F is the most electronegative of F, Cl, Br, I
So H–F is most polar
Answer: H–F
quiz.mistake: Picks the longest bond as the most polar

quiz.q: CCl₄ contains four polar C–Cl bonds. Why is it a non-polar molecule?
options: Its tetrahedral symmetry makes the four bond dipoles cancel
quiz.explain: Four equal dipoles arranged tetrahedrally add to zero.
steps: CCl₄ is tetrahedral with four equal C–Cl dipoles
In a symmetric tetrahedron they add to zero
So the molecule is non-polar
Answer: Its tetrahedral symmetry makes the four bond dipoles cancel
quiz.mistake: Confuses bond polarity with molecular polarity

quiz.q: Which molecule has a non-zero dipole moment?
quiz.explain: In CHCl₃ one C–H bond replaces a C–Cl bond, breaking the symmetry so the dipoles no longer cancel.
steps: CH₄, CCl₄ (tetrahedral) and CO₂ (linear) are symmetric → μ = 0
In CHCl₃ one C–H replaces a C–Cl, breaking the symmetry
So CHCl₃ has μ ≠ 0
Answer: CHCl₃
quiz.mistake: Thinks every tetrahedral molecule is non-polar

quiz.q: Assertion (A): BeF₂ has zero dipole moment. Reason (R): Be–F bonds are non-polar.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true because BeF₂ is linear and the two equal bond dipoles cancel. R is false: Be–F bonds are strongly polar.
steps: Check A: BeF₂ has zero dipole moment: true (linear, dipoles cancel)
Check R: Be–F bonds are non-polar: false, they are strongly polar
So A true, R false
Answer: A is true but R is false
quiz.mistake: Thinks zero dipole moment means the bonds are non-polar

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'CO₂ and H₂O both have polar bonds. Why is only water polar?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! Linear CO₂ cancels its bond dipoles while bent water adds them into a net dipole moment. Gappu bends a stream of water to celebrate!
teach.nudge: Good! How do the shapes of CO₂ and H₂O differ, and what happens to bond dipoles in each?

revise.summary: Bonds between atoms of different electronegativity are polar, and dipole moment μ = Q × r measures this. A molecule's net dipole moment depends on its shape, so symmetrical molecules can have μ = 0.
focus: Polar versus non-polar bonds
Calculate dipole moment and know the debye
Predict zero or non-zero μ from shape
Explain why NH₃ has a larger μ than NF₃
remember: μ = 0: BeF₂, CO₂, BF₃, CH₄, CCl₄
μ(H₂O) = 1.85 D; NH₃ 1.47 D > NF₃ 0.23 D
traps: Don't assume polar bonds make a polar molecule; shape decides
Don't think zero dipole moment means the bonds are non-polar
Don't think every tetrahedral molecule is non-polar; CHCl₃ is polar

topics.title: VSEPR theory and molecular shapes

learn.hook: Electron pairs around an atom behave like people in a crowded Mumbai local: they spread out as far as they possibly can, and the bulky ones (lone pairs) push hardest.
points: VSEPR theory (Sidgwick and Powell, 1940; developed by Nyholm and Gillespie, 1957): the shape of a molecule depends on the number of valence-shell electron pairs (bonded and lone) around the central atom. Pairs repel and arrange themselves as far apart as possible. A multiple bond counts as a single super pair.
Repulsion order: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair, because lone pairs are held by only one nucleus and spread out more.
No lone pairs: 2 pairs linear 180° (BeCl₂); 3 trigonal planar 120° (BF₃); 4 tetrahedral 109.5° (CH₄, NH₄⁺); 5 trigonal bipyramidal 90° and 120° (PCl₅); 6 octahedral 90° (SF₆).

With lone pairs: AB₂E bent (SO₂, O₃); AB₃E trigonal pyramidal (NH₃, 107°); AB₂E₂ bent (H₂O, 104.5°); AB₄E see-saw (SF₄); AB₃E₂ T-shaped (ClF₃); AB₅E square pyramidal (BrF₅); AB₄E₂ square planar (XeF₄).

Method: count valence electrons of the central atom, add one per bonded monovalent atom (and adjust for charge), halve to get total pairs; subtract bond pairs to get lone pairs; pick the arrangement, then describe the shape by the atoms only.

example.q: Predict the shape of ClF₃.
steps: Cl has 7 valence electrons; 3 F atoms contribute 3 → 10 electrons = 5 pairs.
3 bond pairs, 2 lone pairs → trigonal bipyramidal arrangement.
Lone pairs take equatorial positions (more room, fewer 90° repulsions).
The three F atoms form a T.

learn.reallife: The bent shape of water, predicted by VSEPR, gives it the polarity that lets it dissolve salts and sugars, which is why your ORS dissolves and why life is water-based.

quiz.q: What is the shape of SF₄?
quiz.explain: S: 6 + 4 = 10 electrons = 5 pairs (4 bond, 1 lone) → AB₄E → see-saw.
steps: 4 bond pairs, 1 lone pair
Shape: see-saw
Answer: See-saw
quiz.mistake: Ignores the lone pair and calls it tetrahedral

quiz.q: How many lone pairs are on the central atom of XeF₄?
quiz.explain: Xe: 8 + 4 = 12 electrons = 6 pairs; 4 are bond pairs, so 2 lone pairs (square planar).
steps: 6 − 4 = 2 lone pairs
Answer: 2
quiz.mistake: Forgets Xe has 8 valence electrons

quiz.q: Why is the bond angle in NH₃ (107°) smaller than in CH₄ (109.5°)?
options: The lone pair on N repels the bond pairs more strongly than bond pairs repel each other
quiz.explain: lp–bp repulsion > bp–bp repulsion, so the N–H bonds are pushed closer.
steps: Both N in NH₃ and C in CH₄ have four electron pairs
N has one lone pair; lp–bp repulsion > bp–bp repulsion
The N–H bonds are pushed closer: 107° < 109.5°
Answer: The lone pair on N repels the bond pairs more strongly than bond pairs repel each other
quiz.mistake: Attributes the angle to hydrogen bonding

quiz.q: Which correctly orders electron-pair repulsions?
quiz.explain: Lone pairs are attached to only one nucleus and occupy more space, so they repel most.
steps: Lone pairs are held by one nucleus and spread out more
So repulsion order: lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp
Answer: lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp
quiz.mistake: Thinks bonding pairs repel more because they hold atoms

quiz.q: What is the shape of the SO₂ molecule?
quiz.explain: S has 3 electron domains (2 bond regions + 1 lone pair) → AB₂E → bent.
steps: S in SO₂: 2 bonding regions + 1 lone pair = 3 electron domains
Type AB₂E → bent shape
Answer: Bent
quiz.mistake: Treats it as linear like CO₂, ignoring the lone pair

quiz.q: In ClF₃, where are the two lone pairs placed in the trigonal bipyramidal arrangement?
quiz.explain: Equatorial positions have fewer 90° neighbours, minimising lone-pair repulsion; this makes the molecule T-shaped.
steps: ClF₃: 3 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs = 5 → trigonal bipyramidal arrangement
Equatorial positions have fewer 90° neighbours, so lone pairs go there
Both lone pairs equatorial → T-shaped
Answer: Both in equatorial positions
quiz.mistake: Puts lone pairs in axial positions

quiz.q: Which pair of species have the same shape?
quiz.explain: Both have four bond pairs and no lone pair on the central atom: tetrahedral.
steps: CH₄: 4 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → tetrahedral
NH₄⁺: 4 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → tetrahedral
Answer: CH₄ and NH₄⁺
quiz.mistake: Matches by number of atoms instead of electron pairs

quiz.q: Assertion (A): XeF₄ is square planar. Reason (R): Its two lone pairs occupy opposite (trans) positions of an octahedron.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Six pairs give an octahedral arrangement; placing the two lone pairs opposite each other minimises lp–lp repulsion and leaves the four F atoms in a square plane.
steps: XeF₄: 4 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs = 6 → octahedral arrangement
Lone pairs opposite each other (trans) minimise lp–lp repulsion
The four F atoms then lie in a square plane: A and R true, R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Puts the lone pairs at 90° to each other

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does VSEPR tell me that water is bent and ammonia is pyramidal?'
teach.praise: Excellent! Count the pairs, let them repel as far as possible, and remember lone pairs push hardest: water is bent and ammonia pyramidal. Gappu is shaping molecules now!
teach.nudge: Close! How many electron pairs does O have in water and N in ammonia, and what do lone pairs do to the shape?

revise.summary: VSEPR theory says electron pairs around a central atom repel and arrange themselves as far apart as possible. Counting bond pairs and lone pairs predicts the shape of a molecule.
focus: Count bond and lone pairs on the central atom
Know shapes with and without lone pairs
Repulsion order and its effect on bond angles
Lone pair positions in ClF₃ and XeF₄
remember: lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp
AB₂E bent (SO₂); AB₃E pyramidal (NH₃, 107°); AB₂E₂ bent (H₂O, 104.5°)

topics.title: Valence bond theory and orbital overlap

learn.hook: Two hydrogen atoms drifting together feel a pull, then a push. At exactly 74 pm the forces balance and a bond is born, releasing 435.8 kJ for every mole.
points: Formation of H₂: as two H atoms approach, new attractive forces (each nucleus attracts both electrons) and repulsive forces (nucleus–nucleus, electron–electron) arise. Attraction dominates at first, so potential energy falls. At 74 pm energy is minimum (the bond length) and 435.8 kJ mol⁻¹ is released; closer than this, repulsion rises steeply.
Orbital overlap concept: a covalent bond forms when half-filled valence orbitals of two atoms overlap and the two electrons pair with opposite spins. Greater overlap gives a stronger bond.
Simple overlap of pure s and p orbitals cannot explain the directional bonds in CH₄ (four identical bonds at 109.5°), NH₃ or H₂O; p orbitals are at 90°. This is why hybridisation is needed.
Overlap can be positive (same phase or sign, leads to bonding), negative (opposite phase, no bond) or zero (orbitals at right angles or with cancelling regions, no bond).

Sigma (σ) bond: head-on (axial) overlap along the internuclear axis: s–s, s–p or p–p. Pi (π) bond: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, with electron density above and below the internuclear axis.

example.q: Identify the type of overlap in H₂, HCl and Cl₂.
steps: H₂: 1s of one H with 1s of the other: s–s, σ bond.
HCl: 1s of H with 3p of Cl, head-on: s–p, σ bond.
Cl₂: 3p of one Cl with 3p of the other, head-on: p–p, σ bond.
example.answer: s–s σ, s–p σ, p–p σ

learn.reallife: Hydrogen fuel-cell buses trialled in Indian cities release energy by breaking H–H and O=O bonds and forming stronger O–H bonds. The 435.8 kJ mol⁻¹ H–H bond enthalpy is a key number in their design.

The minimum is at 74 pm, the H–H bond length

quiz.q: According to valence bond theory, a covalent bond forms when:
options: Half-filled orbitals of two atoms overlap and their electrons pair with opposite spins

steps: VBT: a bond forms when half-filled orbitals of two atoms overlap
The two electrons pair with opposite spins
Answer: Half-filled orbitals of two atoms overlap and their electrons pair with opposite spins
quiz.mistake: Thinks filled orbitals overlap to form ordinary covalent bonds

options: Positive overlap (orbitals of the same phase)
s–s overlap of the same phase
Head-on overlap of p orbitals of the same phase
quiz.explain: Opposite phases cancel electron density between nuclei, so no bond forms.
steps: Overlap of orbitals with the same phase builds electron density → bond
Opposite phases cancel density between nuclei (negative overlap) → no bond
Answer: Negative overlap (orbitals of opposite phase)
quiz.mistake: Thinks any overlap gives a bond

quiz.q: Why could simple valence bond theory not explain the shape of CH₄?
options: Pure p orbitals are at 90°, but CH₄ has four identical bonds at 109.5°
quiz.explain: Using one 2s and three 2p orbitals directly would give unequal bonds and 90° angles; hybridisation solves this.
steps: Pure 2p orbitals are at 90° to each other
CH₄ has four identical bonds at 109.5°
Simple VBT cannot explain this without hybridisation
Answer: Pure p orbitals are at 90°, but CH₄ has four identical bonds at 109.5°
quiz.mistake: Thinks orbital overlap alone predicts tetrahedral geometry

quiz.q: A π bond is formed by:
options: Head-on overlap of s and p orbitals
Sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals
quiz.explain: π bonds have electron density above and below the internuclear axis from lateral p–p overlap.
steps: A π bond forms by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals
Density lies above and below the bond axis
Answer: Sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals
quiz.mistake: Thinks π bonds lie along the bond axis

quiz.q: Why does potential energy decrease as two hydrogen atoms first approach each other?
options: New attractive forces between each nucleus and both electrons exceed the new repulsive forces
quiz.explain: At moderate distances, nucleus–electron attractions dominate over nucleus–nucleus and electron–electron repulsions.
steps: At moderate distance, new attractions (each nucleus with both electrons) appear
These outweigh the new repulsions (nucleus–nucleus, electron–electron)
So energy falls
Answer: New attractive forces between each nucleus and both electrons exceed the new repulsive forces
quiz.mistake: Ignores the attractive forces between atoms

quiz.q: What type of overlap forms the bond in HF?
options: s–p head-on, giving a σ bond
p–p sideways, giving a π bond
quiz.explain: H uses 1s and F uses a half-filled 2p orbital along the bond axis.
steps: H uses its 1s orbital; F uses a half-filled 2p orbital
They overlap head-on along the bond axis
This is s–p overlap giving a σ bond
Answer: s–p head-on, giving a σ bond
quiz.mistake: Thinks H can use a p orbital

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Energy is released when an H–H bond forms. Reason (R): The system reaches a minimum of potential energy at the bond length.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Going from separated atoms (zero) to the minimum (−435.8 kJ mol⁻¹) releases that energy.
steps: Check A: energy is released when an H–H bond forms: true
Check R: the system reaches minimum potential energy at the bond length: true
Going from zero to −435.8 kJ mol⁻¹ releases energy, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks bond formation needs energy

σ versus π overlap

Positive overlap bonds; negative and zero overlap do not
σ: head-on along the axis; π: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals
traps: Don't confuse the H covalent radius (37 pm) with the bond length (74 pm)
Don't think any overlap gives a bond
Don't think bond formation needs energy; energy is released

topics.title: Strength of σ and π bonds; introducing hybridisation

learn.hook: In ethyne, H–C≡C–H, five bonds hold four atoms. Counting σ and π bonds is one of the most common one-mark questions in boards and JEE.
points: A σ bond is stronger than a π bond, because head-on overlap is larger than sideways overlap. A single bond is one σ; a double bond is 1σ + 1π; a triple bond is 1σ + 2π. A π bond always forms in addition to a σ bond.
Counting: every single bond = 1σ; add 1π for each double bond and 2π for each triple bond. Ethene C₂H₄: 5σ, 1π. Ethyne C₂H₂: 3σ, 2π. CO₂: 2σ, 2π. Benzene C₆H₆: 12σ, 3π.
Hybridisation (Pauling): intermixing of atomic orbitals of slightly different energies on the same atom to form an equal number of new, equivalent hybrid orbitals of identical energy and shape.

Features: the number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed; hybrid orbitals are directed to keep apart as far as possible (minimum repulsion); they overlap more effectively and form stronger bonds than pure orbitals.
Conditions: only valence-shell orbitals hybridise; the orbitals must have almost equal energy; promotion of an electron is not essential, and filled as well as half-filled orbitals can take part.

example.q: Count σ and π bonds in HCN (H–C≡N).
steps: H–C is a single bond: 1σ.
C≡N is a triple bond: 1σ + 2π.
Total: 2σ and 2π.

learn.reallife: Acrylonitrile (CH₂=CH–C≡N), made in Gujarat's petrochemical plants for acrylic fibres in sweaters, has 6σ and 3π bonds; its reactive π bonds are where polymerisation happens.

games.title: Hybridisation features: true or false?
items: The number of hybrid orbitals formed equals the number of atomic orbitals that mix
Hybrid orbitals of one set have different energies
They are equivalent in energy and shape.
Only orbitals of nearly equal energy can hybridise
This is a condition for hybridisation.
Promotion of an electron is essential before hybridisation
Promotion is not essential; even filled orbitals can hybridise.
A π bond can exist between two atoms without a σ bond
A π bond always forms in addition to a σ bond.

quiz.q: How many σ bonds are there in ethene, C₂H₄?
quiz.explain: Four C–H σ bonds + one C–C σ bond (the C=C also has one π) = 5σ.
steps: C–H: 4σ
C=C: 1σ + 1π
Total σ = 5
Answer: 5
quiz.mistake: Counts the double bond as 2σ

quiz.q: How many σ and π bonds are in ethyne, C₂H₂?
quiz.explain: Two C–H σ bonds + C≡C (1σ + 2π) = 3σ, 2π.
steps: Ethyne: H–C≡C–H
2 C–H bonds = 2σ; C≡C = 1σ + 2π
Total = 3σ and 2π
Answer: 3σ and 2π
quiz.mistake: Counts the triple bond as 3π

quiz.q: How many σ bonds are in benzene, C₆H₆?
quiz.explain: Six C–C σ bonds in the ring and six C–H σ bonds = 12σ (plus 3π).
steps: Ring C–C: 6σ
C–H: 6σ
Total = 12
Answer: 12

quiz.q: Why is a σ bond stronger than a π bond?
options: π bonds are formed by s orbitals
Head-on overlap is greater than sideways overlap
quiz.explain: The extent of orbital overlap decides bond strength; axial overlap is larger.
steps: Bond strength depends on the extent of orbital overlap
Head-on (axial) overlap is greater than sideways overlap
So σ bonds are stronger
Answer: Head-on overlap is greater than sideways overlap
quiz.mistake: Thinks σ bonds contain more electrons

quiz.q: Which is a condition for hybridisation?
options: Only completely filled orbitals can hybridise
The orbitals mixing must have almost equal energy
quiz.explain: Hybridisation involves valence orbitals of nearly equal energy on the same atom.
steps: Hybridisation mixes valence orbitals of the same atom
These orbitals must have almost equal energy
Answer: The orbitals mixing must have almost equal energy
quiz.mistake: Confuses hybridisation (on one atom) with overlap (between atoms)

quiz.q: How many σ and π bonds are in CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂ (buta-1,3-diene)?
quiz.explain: Six C–H σ + three C–C σ = 9σ; two C=C each add one π = 2π.
steps: C–H bonds: 6
C–C links: 3 (each 1σ)
Double bonds: 2 → 2π
σ bonds = 6 + 3 = 9; π bonds = 2
Answer: 9σ and 2π
quiz.mistake: Counts each double bond as 2σ

quiz.q: When one s and two p orbitals hybridise, how many hybrid orbitals form?

steps: Number of hybrid orbitals = number of atomic orbitals mixed
1 s + 2 p = 3 orbitals
So 3 sp² orbitals
Answer: 3

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Rotation about a C=C double bond is restricted. Reason (R): Rotation would break the sideways overlap of the π bond.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A

steps: Check A: rotation about C=C is restricted: true
Check R: rotation would break the sideways π overlap: true
R explains A: the π bond needs parallel p orbitals

topics.title: sp, sp², sp³ and d-orbital hybridisation

learn.hook: The same carbon atom becomes a tetrahedron in methane, a flat triangle in ethene and a straight line in ethyne. Hybridisation is carbon's shape-shifting trick.
points: sp: one s + one p → two sp orbitals at 180° (linear), 50% s character. BeCl₂ (Be: 2s² → 2s¹2p¹, then sp). Carbon in C₂H₂ is sp; the two unhybridised p orbitals form two π bonds (C≡C 120 pm).
sp²: one s + two p → three sp² orbitals at 120° (trigonal planar), 33.3% s character. BCl₃; carbon in C₂H₄ (the unhybridised p forms the π bond; C=C 134 pm).
sp³: one s + three p → four sp³ orbitals at 109.5° (tetrahedral), 25% s character. CH₄; also NH₃ (one lone pair in an sp³ orbital, 107°) and H₂O (two lone pairs, 104.5°).

sp³d: five orbitals → trigonal bipyramidal, as in PCl₅. Three equatorial P–Cl bonds lie in a plane at 120°; two axial bonds lie at 90° to that plane. Axial bonds suffer more repulsion and are slightly longer, which makes PCl₅ reactive. sp³d²: six orbitals → octahedral, as in SF₆. dsp²: square planar, as in [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻.
To predict: count σ bond pairs + lone pairs on the central atom (steric number): 2 → sp, 3 → sp², 4 → sp³, 5 → sp³d, 6 → sp³d².

example.q: Predict the hybridisation and geometry of the central atom in PCl₅ and in NH₃.
steps: PCl₅: P has 5 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → steric number 5 → sp³d, trigonal bipyramidal.
NH₃: N has 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair → steric number 4 → sp³.
With one lone pair, NH₃'s shape is trigonal pyramidal (107°).
example.answer: PCl₅: sp³d, trigonal bipyramidal; NH₃: sp³, trigonal pyramidal

learn.reallife: SF₆, an sp³d² octahedral molecule, is so stable and non-reactive that power grids, including India's high-voltage substations, use it as an insulating gas in switchgear.

quiz.q: What is the hybridisation of oxygen in H₂O?
quiz.explain: O has 2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs = 4 electron domains → sp³; the shape is bent with angle 104.5°.

4 domains → sp³ hybridisation

Answer: sp³

Answer: 33.33

quiz.explain: Each axial bond pair is at 90° to three equatorial pairs, so it is repelled more and is pushed slightly farther out.

So axial pairs face more repulsion
They are pushed out and become slightly longer

quiz.mistake: Thinks all five bonds of PCl₅ are identical

quiz.q: What are the hybridisation and geometry of SF₆?
quiz.explain: Six S–F bond pairs and no lone pair need six hybrid orbitals: sp³d², octahedral.
steps: S in SF₆: 6 bond pairs, no lone pair
6 hybrid orbitals needed: s + 3p + 2d = sp³d²

Answer: sp³d², octahedral

quiz.q: The carbon atoms in ethyne are sp hybridised. What is the H–C–C bond angle?

steps: sp hybridisation gives two orbitals pointing opposite ways
So the molecule is linear
H–C–C angle = 180°

quiz.q: Which molecule has an sp²-hybridised central atom?

steps: B in BF₃: 3 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → 3 hybrid orbitals → sp²
CH₄ and NH₃ are sp³; BeCl₂ is sp

quiz.q: In ethene, which orbitals form the C=C π bond?
quiz.explain: Each carbon keeps one unhybridised 2p orbital perpendicular to the molecular plane; these overlap sideways to form the π bond.
steps: Each carbon in ethene is sp² and keeps one unhybridised 2p orbital
These 2p orbitals overlap sideways to form the π bond
The sp² orbitals form the σ bonds
Answer: Unhybridised 2p orbitals on each carbon
quiz.mistake: Thinks hybrid orbitals form π bonds

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The C≡C bond (120 pm) is shorter than the C=C bond (134 pm). Reason (R): sp orbitals have more s character than sp² orbitals and hold electrons closer to the nucleus.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Higher s character makes hybrid orbitals smaller and more compact, so bonds formed by sp carbon are shorter (together with the higher bond order).
steps: sp has 50% s character; sp² has 33%
More s character → orbital held closer to the nucleus → shorter bond
So C≡C (sp) is shorter than C=C (sp²): A and R true, R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks s character has no effect on bond length

topics.title: Molecular orbital theory: LCAO, bonding and antibonding orbitals

learn.hook: Valence bond theory says O₂ has all electrons paired, yet liquid oxygen sticks between the poles of a magnet. Molecular orbital theory explains what VBT cannot.
points: Salient features (Mulliken, Hund): electrons in a molecule occupy molecular orbitals (MOs) spread over the whole molecule (polycentric), not atomic orbitals. Atomic orbitals of comparable energy and proper symmetry combine to form MOs; the number of MOs formed equals the number of atomic orbitals combined. MOs are filled by the Aufbau principle, Pauli principle and Hund's rule.
LCAO (linear combination of atomic orbitals): ψ_MO = ψ_A ± ψ_B. Addition (ψ_A + ψ_B) gives a bonding MO (σ); subtraction (ψ_A − ψ_B) gives an antibonding MO (σ*).

Bonding MO: electron density concentrated between the nuclei, lower energy than the parent atomic orbitals, stabilises the molecule. Antibonding MO: a nodal plane between the nuclei where density is zero, higher energy, destabilises the molecule.

Conditions for combination: the atomic orbitals must have comparable energy, the same symmetry about the molecular axis (taken as z), and should overlap as much as possible. 2pz on one atom cannot combine with 2px on the other.
Types: σ MOs are symmetrical about the bond axis (from 1s, 2s and 2pz); π MOs are not (from 2px and 2py), with electron density above and below the axis. Each has an antibonding partner: σ*, π*.

example.q: Two 1s orbitals of hydrogen combine. How many MOs form, and what are they?
steps: Two atomic orbitals combine → two molecular orbitals.
ψ₁ₛ(A) + ψ₁ₛ(B) → σ1s, the bonding MO (lower energy).
ψ₁ₛ(A) − ψ₁ₛ(B) → σ*1s, the antibonding MO (higher energy, node between nuclei).

learn.reallife: MO theory is the language of materials scientists at IITs designing organic solar cells and OLED displays, where the gap between the highest filled and lowest empty MOs decides the colour and efficiency.

steps: Rule: number of MOs formed = number of atomic orbitals combined
4 AOs → 4 MOs
Answer: 4

quiz.q: Which statement about an antibonding molecular orbital is correct?
options: It has maximum electron density between the nuclei
It is formed by addition of wave functions
It has a node between the nuclei and higher energy than the parent atomic orbitals
quiz.explain: Subtracting wave functions cancels density between nuclei, creating a node and raising the energy.
steps: Antibonding MO: ψ_A − ψ_B (subtraction)
Electron density cancels between nuclei → a node
Its energy is higher than the parent AOs
Answer: It has a node between the nuclei and higher energy than the parent atomic orbitals
quiz.mistake: Mixes up bonding and antibonding features

quiz.q: Which pair of atomic orbitals CANNOT combine if z is the molecular axis?
quiz.explain: 2pz and 2px have different symmetry about the z-axis, so their net overlap is zero.
steps: AOs combine only if they have the same symmetry about the bond (z) axis
2pz is symmetric along z; 2px is not
Their net overlap is zero, so they cannot combine
Answer: 2pz and 2px
quiz.mistake: Ignores the symmetry condition

quiz.q: A bonding molecular orbital is formed by:
options: Overlap of orbitals of very different energies
Addition of atomic wave functions, ψ_A + ψ_B
quiz.explain: Constructive interference increases electron density between the nuclei.
steps: Bonding MO = ψ_A + ψ_B (addition)
Constructive interference increases density between nuclei
Answer: Addition of atomic wave functions, ψ_A + ψ_B
quiz.mistake: Reverses addition and subtraction

quiz.q: Which is a salient feature of molecular orbital theory?
options: Electrons stay in the atomic orbitals of their own atoms
A molecular orbital is influenced by two or more nuclei
The number of MOs is half the number of AOs
quiz.explain: MOs are polycentric; electrons in them belong to the molecule as a whole.
steps: In MO theory an MO is spread over two or more nuclei (polycentric)
Electrons belong to the molecule as a whole
Answer: A molecular orbital is influenced by two or more nuclei
quiz.mistake: Applies the valence bond picture to MO theory

quiz.q: Why can the 1s orbital of one atom not combine effectively with the 2s orbital of an identical neighbouring atom?
quiz.explain: Only atomic orbitals of comparable energy combine to an appreciable extent.
steps: AOs combine effectively only if their energies are comparable
1s and 2s of identical atoms differ greatly in energy
Answer: Their energies are too different
quiz.mistake: Thinks symmetry is the problem for two s orbitals

quiz.q: Which molecular orbital is formed from sideways combination of 2px orbitals?
quiz.explain: With z as the bond axis, 2px orbitals overlap sideways to give π2px (bonding) and π*2px (antibonding).
steps: With z as the bond axis, 2px orbitals are perpendicular to it
They overlap sideways → π2px (bonding) and π*2px
Answer: π2px
quiz.mistake: Thinks every p combination gives a σ orbital

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Electrons in bonding MOs stabilise a molecule. Reason (R): Bonding MOs have higher energy than the atomic orbitals from which they form.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: bonding MOs are lower in energy than the parent atomic orbitals, which is why they stabilise the molecule.
steps: Check A: electrons in bonding MOs stabilise a molecule: true
Check R: bonding MOs are higher in energy than the parent AOs: false, they are lower
So A true, R false
Answer: A is true but R is false
quiz.mistake: Reverses the energies of bonding MOs and atomic orbitals
